Anna Vaudano, Helmut Laufs, Stefan Kiebel, and colleagues mapped seizure signals in the brain for PLOS ONE in 2009. Generalised spike and wave discharges are the EEG hallmark of absence seizures. During these seizures, ongoing activity stops briefly and awareness fades. The discharges involve a network linking the thalamus and the cortex.

The team asked about causal hierarchy inside that network during the discharges. Which structure drives, and which follows, matters for treatment. Stimulation or surgery works better when aimed at the true driver. Their analysis of brain recordings offers evidence on the order of events in absence seizures.
plos-pone-0006575:
Jane Palsgaard and co-authors read gene activity in muscle from people with diabetes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gene expression alterations have previously been associated with type 2 diabetes. However, whether these changes are primary causes or secondary effects of the disease is unclear. The team took skeletal muscle biopsies from people with type 2 diabetes and their relatives.

Studying relatives helps, since they share genes but not yet disease. Their title highlights differential regulation of specific metabolic pathways. Changes present in healthy relatives may be causes; changes only in patients may be effects. That logic is key to finding where diabetes begins.
plos-pone-0006675:
Jonathan Levy and colleagues used brain imaging to test a theory of reading in PLOS ONE in 2009. The dual-route cascade model describes how readers turn print into sound and meaning. Evidence for the model came largely from people with acquired reading problems. Brain lesions in those patients are often large and varied, which limits firm conclusions.

The team turned to functional magnetic resonance imaging in healthy readers. They measured effective connectivity, meaning how brain regions influence each other during reading. Their account centers on an efficient reading style. The results let them check the model's predictions in an intact brain. That gives reading science a cleaner test than patient studies alone can offer.
plos-pone-0006775:
Masja Leendertse and her team asked if gut germs change lung defense in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. The germ was Enterococcus faecium, found more and more in hospital patients. Drug-proof strains of it are a growing worry. It is tied to more illness from gut germs of its own kind. It might also make lung illness worse.

The team let the germ settle in mouse guts. They then put a second germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in the lungs. Gut carriage did not change lung defense, as the title states. That clear no narrows where gut carriage does its harm. Lung defense held firm even when the gut held drug-proof germs.
plos-pone-0006875:
Xiangning Chen and colleagues followed a cell-death cleanup pathway into schizophrenia genetics in PLOS ONE in 2009. Apoptosis, programmed cell death, has been speculated to play a role. Their earlier study linked the gene MEGF10 to the disease. MEGF10 helps cells engulf dead neighbors. Partners in that pathway include GULP1, ABCA1, and ABCA7.

The team tested those pathway genes for association with schizophrenia. Testing a whole pathway is stronger than testing one gene. Shared involvement would tie brain development to cleanup failures. Leftover dead cells could disturb developing circuits. The study extends a single-gene hint into a pathway-level claim.
plos-pone-0006975:
Tobias Karlberg, Susanne van den Berg, Martin Hammarström, and colleagues solved a protein structure in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein was paraplegin, part of a protease in the inner membrane of mitochondria. Faults in paraplegin cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, a disease that stiffens the legs. The protein is thought to form a six-part ring that burns ATP for power.

The team crystallized the ATPase domain, the part that uses that fuel. They then determined its three-dimensional shape. A clear structure shows where disease mutations fall. It also gives drug and protein engineers a map of this molecular machine.
plos-pone-0007075:
Adaikkalam Vellaichamy, Arun Sreekumar, John Strahler, and colleagues mapped androgen action in prostate cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in American men. Advanced hormone-refractory cases still had no cure at the time. Part of the problem was poor knowledge of the proteins androgens control.

Using proteomics, the team catalogued proteins that shift with androgen action. Aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, the enzymes that load transfer RNAs, stood out. Their appearance links hormone signaling to the cell's protein-making machinery. That link offers new places to probe how these cancers keep growing.
plos-pone-0007175:
Jerome Mauris and Thomas C. Evans published a 2009 PLOS ONE study of a DNA repair enzyme from a heat-loving bacterium. The bacterium is Aquifex aeolicus, and the enzyme is its MutL protein. MutL helps cut DNA near errors during mismatch repair, the process that fixes wrongly paired bases.

The authors test how adenosine triphosphate, the cell energy molecule called ATP, changes MutL activity. Earlier work had shown ATP was needed for related proteins in humans and yeast. Their results clarify how a simple energy molecule switches on an early step in DNA repair.
plos-pone-0007275:
Joanna Doumanis, Koji Wada, Yoshihiro Kino, and colleagues screened fruit fly cells for modifiers of a disease protein in 2009. The fruit fly is a well established model for human neurodegenerative diseases. Mutant huntingtin protein forms aggregates, clumps that mark Huntington disease in patients.

The authors use RNA interference to turn genes down one by one. They run a high-throughput screen in fly larval brain-derived cells expressing mutant huntingtin. They identify new modifiers of aggregate formation. Each new modifier is a candidate target for easing protein clumping in human neurons.
plos-pone-0007375:
Fabienne Paumet, Jordan Wesolowski, Alejandro Garcia-Diaz, and colleagues found virus-like fusion tools inside bacteria in 2009. Pathogens use diverse molecular machines to enter host cells and manipulate vesicle traffic. Viruses use glycoproteins similar to SNARE proteins, the cell's own fusion machinery, to merge membranes during entry into host cells.

Intracellular bacteria take another route into cells. The authors report that intracellular bacteria encode inhibitory SNARE-like proteins. These proteins can block normal membrane fusion inside the host. Blocking fusion helps bacteria avoid being delivered to destructive compartments. Their finding reveals a subtle weapon in intracellular infection.
plos-pone-0007475:
Darrell Pilling and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on fibrocytes, blood-born cells that help form scar tissue. In scar diseases, white blood cells called monocytes enter tissue and turn into fiber-making cells. The trouble is telling those cells apart from close kin. Monocytes also become macrophages, and fibrocytes look much like plain fibroblasts. Without good markers, the scar-making cells are hard to track.

The team found markers that set fibrocytes apart from monocytes, macrophages, and fibroblasts. Those tags let researchers count and sort the right cells in samples. Clear naming makes every study of scarring stronger. It also helps test drugs meant to stop scars from forming. The work is a sorting tool, but a needed one for the whole field.
plos-pone-0007575:
Anna Gustafsson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common form of kidney cancer. The disease's molecular biology is complex and not fully understood. The team had earlier found that a receptor called Axl, found on tumors, correlates with patient survival on its own. Here they investigated Axl together with Gas6, the molecule that activates it.

A receptor and its activator acting as a pair can drive tumor behavior. Measuring both in tumors sharpens what Axl alone suggests. The signaling pair may help explain why some kidney cancers turn more dangerous than others. Such pairs are attractive drug targets, since blocking either partner can break the signal. The study deepens the case for Axl in kidney cancer prognosis and treatment thinking.
plos-pone-0007775:
John Ludes-Meyers and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It delivers a new mouse tool for studying a tumor suppressor gene called Wwox. The gene spans a fragile stretch of chromosome that breaks often in human cells. Wwox is switched off in many cancers and can slow tumor growth.

The team built mice carrying a conditional copy of the gene. Conditional means the gene can be turned off in chosen tissues or at chosen times. They describe how the mice were made and tested. The model lets researchers ask what Wwox does in healthy tissue and in tumors.
plos-pone-0007875:
Melanie Volke and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a claim about hepcidin, the hormone that controls iron in the body. Hepcidin limits iron uptake from food and locks iron away in stores. It plays a key role in the anemia that comes with chronic disease.

Low oxygen is known to lower hepcidin levels. Factors that sense low oxygen, called HIFs, were suspected of switching the gene off directly. The authors present evidence against that direct suppression. Their result redirects the search for how oxygen controls iron, an everyday balance with real effects on health.
plos-pone-0007975:
Ismayil Ahmet and colleagues fed blueberries to rats with weak hearts in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. The rats had dilated hearts after a heart attack, a state like human heart failure. Past work had hinted that berry-rich food guards heart tissue.

Rats on the berry diet lived longer and kept stronger hearts than rats on plain food. The gain held over the long term, not just the first weeks. Food alone will not cure heart failure, but the work backs the idea that plant compounds in the diet can help a struggling heart hold on.
plos-pone-0008075:
Jeffrey Mito and colleagues matched a mouse tumor to its human twin by gene pattern in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human cancer is a soft tissue sarcoma. It has no clear cell of origin. Its old name frankly admitted that doctors cannot tell what it is. Mouse models existed, but which human disease they truly mirror was in doubt.

Gene profiles from the mouse tumors lined up with the human sarcoma called undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma. With the match firm, lab results from the mouse can be read with more trust. A good stand-in is half the battle in testing new drugs for a rare cancer.
plos-pone-0008175:
Louise V. Wain and co-authors published a genome-wide study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. ALS destroys the nerve cells that control muscle movement. Most cases arise with no clear family history. The team asked whether extra or missing copies of DNA stretches help explain who develops the disease.

The authors scanned genomes for these copy changes, called copy number variants. They then compared their results with gene sites reported in earlier work. Two past studies had hinted that copy changes may raise risk for cases without a family link. Testing that hint at genome scale helps show where gene dose may matter. It also gives later teams a checked set of sites worth testing again.
plos-pone-0008275:
Marie Ballif and colleagues studied HIV treatment outcomes in Switzerland in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Combination antiretroviral therapy has been very successful in clinical trials. Real-world results across a whole population can differ from trial results. Prior treatment failures and poor adherence may weaken outcomes. The team described therapy results in 2007 in a large national cohort.

They drew on the Swiss HIV cohort, which follows patients across the country. Knowing how past failures and missed doses affect success guides care. It also helps programs support patients before resistance builds. The study gives a population-level picture of treatment in practice.
plos-pone-0008375:
Pascaline J. Le Gouar and colleagues studied Ebola's effect on gorillas in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Emerging infectious diseases threaten both human health and biodiversity. An outbreak can slash a wildlife population quickly. Beyond deaths, disease can erode genetic diversity in survivors. Lower diversity raises a species' risk of extinction later.

The team examined how an Ebola outbreak changed the genetics of western lowland gorilla populations. Comparing diversity before and after shows the hidden cost of epidemics. Conservation plans must account for that genetic damage. The work links disease ecology to long-term survival of apes.
plos-pone-0008475:
Therese Andersson and co-authors study fat tissue and menopause in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. With age and menopause, fat shifts in women. It moves from hips and thighs to the belly. That shift raises risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease. Hormones called glucocorticoids shape where fat is stored. An enzyme known as 11beta-HSD1 boosts those hormones in tissue.

The team measure this enzyme in fat from normal weight women after menopause. They find tissue-specific increases in its activity. Those increases may help drive the belly fat shift. The work links a local enzyme change to a whole body pattern.
plos-pone-0008575:
Guido Santilli, Giuseppe Lamorte, Luigi Carlessi, and colleagues published a stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neural stem cells can grow into several kinds of brain cell, so labs prize them for studying diseases that destroy nerve tissue. The team used a human line kept alive with a v-myc gene. Those cells still behaved much like normal parent stem cells.

Oxygen levels around growing cells proved decisive in their tests. Gently lowering oxygen helped the stem cells multiply faster. It also helped them keep multipotency, the power to become more than one cell type. Standard lab air may therefore be a poor match for the brain. Their results point growers toward low-oxygen culture for future repair work.
plos-pone-0008675:
Damian Kovalovsky and co-authors build a T cell model in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A complete understanding of negative selection has been elusive. Negative selection deletes self-reactive T cells in the thymus. Those cells die rapidly and are cleared in vivo, hiding the process. The team report a novel TCR transgenic model. In it, T cell receptor expression during differentiation occurs only after V(D)J-like recombination, mimicking natural timing.

Their model reveals negative selection involves two pathways. An immediate pathway depends on Bim, a death protein. A delayed pathway proceeds independently of Bim. Two routes ensure self-reactive cells are removed thoroughly. The model opens negative selection to direct study.
plos-pone-0008775:
Jean Woo, Ruth Chan, Jason Leung, and colleagues weighed what shapes health in old age. Their survey study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Four thousand people aged sixty-five and older answered a health survey. Outcomes included quality of life, frailty, and death. Place, money, and daily habits all might matter. Few studies had compared their weights directly, especially for frailty.

The analysis separated geographic, social, and lifestyle contributions. Each factor family explained a distinct share of the outcomes. Lifestyle and social conditions stood out as changeable levers. The breakdown helps governments target healthy-aging programs where they help most.
plos-pone-0008875:
John Craft, Jack Gilbert, Ben Temperton, and colleagues read gene messages across the body parts of a sea mussel. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mussels of the Mytilus group anchor marine ecology studies. They also serve as living sensors of water quality. Their molecular biology, oddly, remained poorly charted. Pyrosequencing could read many gene messages fast.

Message profiles differed sharply between tissues of Mytilus galloprovincialis. Each body part ran its own gene program. The tissue map supports studies of reproduction, hybridization, and pollution response. Environmental monitoring gains a molecular toolkit for a sentinel species.
plos-pone-0008975:
Zhumur Ghosh and co-authors compared lab-made stem cells with true embryonic ones, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Induced pluripotent stem cells are adult cells pushed back to an embryo-like state. They dodge the ethical fights around embryo use and could match a patient's own tissue. Still, small differences from embryonic stem cells had been noticed.

The team found that some donor-cell genes stay switched on in the reprogrammed cells. That leftover activity from the original adult cell sets the two cell types apart. The donor memory fades with time in culture but never matched at the start. Knowing the gap exists helps labs judge which cell lines suit research or therapy.
plos-pone-0009075:
Ying Wai Lam and co-authors listed the proteins tagged by a signalling gas in prostate cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nitric oxide is a gas cells use as a short-range signal. Enzymes making it are overactive in several prostate diseases. The gas tags proteins by S-nitrosylation, attaching to sulfur atoms.

The team mapped those tags across prostate epithelial cells. They identified the target proteins and the exact tagged sites. Key regulators of cell signalling carried many of the tags. The catalogue gives prostate research new leads on how the gas does harm.
plos-pone-0009175:
Ulrike Naumann and co-authors gave an odd chemokine receptor a clean-up job, in PLOS ONE in 2010. CXCR7 is a second receptor for the signalling molecule CXCL12. It looks like a normal signalling receptor but fails to fire the usual pathway. Its real function was still openly debated when the study ran.

The team showed CXCR7 quietly scavenges CXCL12 and its cousin CXCL11. It pulls those signals out of circulation without answering them itself. A silent sponge like this can shape where immune cells travel. Receptors that only clear signals turn out to be regulators in their own right.
plos-pone-0009275:
Rajesh Katare and co-authors published this heart study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Studying heart disease is easier with a good lab model. Engineered heart tissue, grown from cells into beating strips, had already proved useful in transplant research. The team asked whether it could also mimic a heart starved of blood.

They showed engineered heart tissue can reproduce the ischemic changes of the heart in a dish. Ischemia, the loss of blood flow behind heart attacks, could then be studied step by step. A controllable model lets researchers test protections that would be risky in patients. The tool brings heart attack biology onto the lab bench.
plos-pone-0009375:
Nicolas Senn and co-authors published this malaria measurement study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging how intense malaria is in a region usually needs parasite surveys. Those are costly and slow. The authors proposed a cheaper signal hiding in blood tests: hemoglobin.

In Papua New Guinea, they compared average hemoglobin and anemia rates against established malaria indicators. Malaria destroys red blood cells, so where it is common, hemoglobin sinks. If the cheap measure tracks the costly ones, health programs gain a handy gauge. It could also help monitor whether control efforts are working.
plos-pone-0009475:
Charles Kimmel, April DeLaurier, and Bonnie Ullmann followed the growth of a zebrafish skull bone in PLOS ONE in 2010. Each bone of the face must reach an exact shape to do its job. Skull shapes also vary a lot between species. The team watched one craniofacial bone as it grew in young fish. They tracked how its edge advanced and how its form was sculpted.

The study sets out the modes by which the bone grows outward. It links cell level moves to the final shape of the bone. That bridge between genes, cells, and form is central to understanding faces. It also helps explain how skull shapes change over evolution.
plos-pone-0009575:
Rajarshi Ghosh and co-authors linked cell stress to blood vessel growth in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growth of new vessels, called angiogenesis, serves both normal development and cancer. A factor named VEGF-A is the chief signal for that growth. Cells under stress, with misfolded proteins piling up, answer through the unfolded protein response. The team asked whether that response can switch on VEGF-A.

They showed the stress pathway does drive the VEGF-A gene. So a strained cell can call for a better blood supply. That link joins two major processes in disease. It matters for cancer, where stressed tumor cells crave vessels, and for other ills as well.
plos-pone-0009675:
Pablo Arias and Javier Cudeiro tested beat based therapy in Parkinson's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Parkinson's can freeze a person's steps mid walk, a symptom called freezing of gait. A steady rhythm sometimes unlocks movement. The team gave rhythmic auditory stimulation, a regular beat, to patients as they walked. They included patients both with and without freezing.

Walking measures changed under the beat, and not in the same way for both groups. Knowing who gains most helps aim the therapy well. A beat costs nothing and carries no drug side effects. The study gives measured support for sound as a tool to keep people with Parkinson's moving.
plos-pone-0009875:
Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach and can, over years, help trigger stomach cancer. Song-Ze Ding and colleagues studied how the bacterium rewrites gene activity in stomach cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The rewriting happens through histone modification, chemical marks on the proteins that spool DNA. The team linked those marks to changed gene expression in gastric epithelial cells. Epithelial cells line the stomach wall where the bacterium settles. Tracing the marks clarifies the bacterium's role in pathogenesis, the making of disease. Stomach cancer remains a major killer worldwide.
plos-pone-0009975:
Crops that make their own insect poison can fail when insects evolve resistance. Silvia Caccia and colleagues found the exact change behind resistance in two moth species. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Moth caterpillars are major cotton and corn pests.

The poison is a Cry2A protein from Bacillus thuringiensis, sprayed and planted worldwide as Bt. Field-isolated resistance means the insects were caught in fields, not bred in labs. Alteration of the binding site, the gut spot the poison must grip, caused the resistance. Both Helicoverpa species shared that route.
plos-pone-0010075:
The authors were William Rice, David Kaplan, and Irene Georgakoudi. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study offered a gentler way to watch stem cells mature. Building working tissues in the lab takes careful control over many stages. Checking progress usually means destroying samples, which wastes time and material.

The team used two-photon microscopy, an imaging method that needs no cutting or staining. It can measure cell differentiation inside living samples in numbers, not just pictures. A non-invasive check like that could help tissue engineers tune growth conditions as they go. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010175:
The authors were Nathan Geething, Wayne To, Benjamin Spink, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study improved a rescue hormone for diabetes care. Most diabetes drugs lower blood sugar, but insulin treatment risks driving it too low. Glucagon raises blood sugar and counters that danger, yet it fades fast and can overshoot baseline levels.

The team created Gcg-XTEN, a longer-acting modified glucagon. In their tests it prevented hypoglycemia, dangerously low blood sugar, without raising baseline glucose. A steadier rescue drug could make intensive insulin therapy safer for patients. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010275:
Jingyuan Deng, Wei Wang, and Long Lu built a computer model of an embryo pattern signal in 2010. Bicoid is a protein that patterns the front structures of fruit fly embryos. It forms a gradient, high at the front and fading backward, that tells cells where they sit. Recent experiments revealed new detail about that gradient's behavior in living embryos.

A model was needed that could recapture the observed behavior faithfully. Their two-dimensional simulation does that in a PLOS ONE paper. Comparing model and embryo can settle debates about how a stable gradient forms from a local source.
plos-pone-0010375:
Ge Zhang and colleagues linked a fat-related gene to body measures on a Croatian island in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, FTO, had already been tied to obesity in many studies. Island populations are useful for genetics: they are often more uniform in ancestry and lifestyle. The team checked whether FTO variants tracked with a wide range of body traits there. Height, weight, and fat measures all counted.

The variants did line up with obesity-related traits in this island group. Repeating a known link in a fresh population strengthens it. It also lets researchers test subtler traits than weight alone. Island studies can reveal gene effects that noisy city samples hide. This one confirms FTO's reach extends to the eastern Adriatic coast.
plos-pone-0010475:
Francesco Cardarelli and Enrico Gratton presented a way to watch single molecules cross the nucleus gate in PLOS ONE in 2010. The nucleus is wrapped in a double membrane pierced by pore complexes. Those pores ferry proteins and RNA in both directions, constantly. Many studies describe traffic through the nucleus broadly. This work proposed measuring the passage of individual molecules through the pores themselves.

Their method uses pair correlation functions, a statistical trick on flickering light signals. It can time single molecules as they transit the pore. Watching one molecule at a time reveals steps that averages hide. Nuclear transport faults are tied to viruses and disease. A sharper measuring tool could clarify many such cases.
plos-pone-0010575:
Noëlla Arnaud and colleagues studied hepatitis C virus for a PLOS ONE paper in 2010. Healthy cells react to virus invasion by making interferon, a signal that warns nearby cells. Hepatitis C triggers surprisingly little interferon, and the team wanted to know why.

Their experiments point to a cell protein called PKR. The virus switches PKR on, and that switch helps hold interferon production down. In effect, the virus turns a defense protein to its own advantage. The finding adds one more step to the picture of how hepatitis C stays quiet in the liver.
plos-pone-0010675:
Laura Denney and colleagues reported immune profiles from three severe cases of 2009 pandemic flu, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most people shook off the new H1N1 virus with mild illness. A few, including one pregnant patient, grew worse fast and died. The team wanted to know what set those cases apart.

Blood tests showed a sharp drop in natural killer cells, an early defense force. Killer CD8 T cells, which attack infected cells, stayed near normal. Losing the first force while keeping the second is a distinct pattern. If larger studies confirm it, a simple cell count might flag flu patients who need close care early.
plos-pone-0010775:
Amare Deribew and colleagues studied malaria and under-nutrition together in young Ethiopian children, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In southwest Ethiopia many children under five face both threats at once. Each condition can worsen the other, yet their overlap in the community had not been well measured.

Health workers examined children in their home area and tested them for malaria. Under-nutrition was common, and it clustered with malaria infection. The two burdens shared the same poorest households. Programs that treat one condition alone will miss much of the harm. The authors argue for combined screening where both are common.
plos-pone-0010875:
Nizar Ibrahim, David Unwin, David Martill and co-authors described a new flying reptile in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Kem Kem beds of southeastern Morocco hold a rich fossil assemblage from the Cretaceous period, but most pterosaur finds there are scraps of teeth and jaw tips. Only one Moroccan pterosaur species had been named before this work.

The team based the new species, Alanqa saharica, on a nearly complete, well-preserved lower jaw joint section, and assigned several other jaw fragments to it. Its jaw is strikingly straight and spear-shaped, with a raised bump near the back of its upper surface. Most specimens suggest a wingspan of roughly three to four meters. Ibrahim and colleagues add a second named pterosaur to Morocco's record and show the region hosted giant, toothless fliers.
plos-pone-0010975:
Mingyu Liu, Edward Schmidt and William Halford published this herpesvirus study in PLOS ONE in 2010. ICP0 is a herpes simplex virus protein studied for twenty-five years as a nuclear regulator that tips the virus between hiding and multiplying. The authors tagged it with a glowing marker to watch where it goes, and got a surprise.

Both tagged and normal ICP0 appeared mainly in the cell's cytoplasm, outside the nucleus, after the earliest phase of infection. There, ICP0 dismantled the cell's microtubule network, the rails used for internal transport. A mutant lacking its enzymatic ring finger bundled the rails instead of dispersing them. Liu and colleagues uncover a second, physical job for a famous viral protein. Rearranging the host cell's skeleton may help the virus assemble or exit, a fresh angle for antiviral thinking.
plos-pone-0011075:
Mathilde Savy, Branwen Hennig, Conor Doherty and co-authors published this child health genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trachoma, a chlamydial eye infection, is the leading infectious cause of blindness, and families differ in susceptibility. Because the bacterium's growth depends on iron, the authors tested two iron-related genetic factors: variants of haptoglobin, which scavenges iron, and the sickle cell trait.

In two surveys of more than eight hundred young children in rural Gambia, about a fifth showed signs of active trachoma. One haptoglobin haplotype doubled the risk of active disease in boys, while pointing the opposite way, though not significantly, in girls, and the sex difference itself was statistically significant. Savy and colleagues show genetic risk for an eye infection can run in opposite directions by sex, complicating any one-size screening rule.
plos-pone-0011175:
Jiang, Ren, Sun and colleagues cloned a crab gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. Leptin is a hormone best known for signaling fullness in mammals. The team isolated the gene for its receptor in the Chinese mitten crab and mapped where in the crab's body the gene is active.

Finding a working leptin receptor in a crab extends this hormone system far beyond mammals. It suggests the system has ancient roots in animal evolution. That broadens comparative studies of appetite and energy balance. The crab is also a farmed species, so growth and feeding knowledge has practical value.
plos-pone-0011275:
Sayama, Kajiya, Sugawara and colleagues studied hair growth in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. A signaling protein best known from inflammation also works in skin. Mice lacking it only in skin cells let the team isolate its role in forming hair follicles and starting new growth phases.

The protein proved to regulate both follicle formation and the induction of active growth. That dual role makes it a hair growth controller worth attention. Hair loss research gains a new molecular entry point. Any future treatment would need care, since the same protein serves the immune system elsewhere.
plos-pone-0011375:
Matthew Brandley and co-authors argued in 2010 that Bermuda shelters an ancient line of lizards found nowhere else. The island's skinks are endangered, and genetic work showed their lineage split from relatives very long ago. Cut off in the Atlantic, Bermuda may have served as a refuge where the line survived while mainland kin vanished.

Treating the island as an evolutionary life raft changes how its lizards are valued. They are not a minor offshoot but the last carriers of a deep branch of lizard history. Losing them would erase far more history than losing a young, widespread species. The paper gives conservationists a strong case for protecting Bermuda's habitats, since a small island can hold a share of life's history out of all proportion to its size.
plos-pone-0011475:
Jason D'Antonio and co-authors untangled in 2010 two effects of the male hormone receptor in prostate cancer. Prostate tumors depend on androgen hormones acting through their receptor, and treatment often blocks that signal. The receptor can also brake tumor growth, and cancers were thought to escape the brake only by becoming addicted to the signal itself.

The team showed those two changes can come apart: cancer cells can lose the receptor's growth suppression without acquiring dependence on receptor signaling. Splitting the roles changes how hormone therapy resistance should be understood and attacked. A tumor that merely lost the brake needs a different counter than one hooked on the signal. For a common cancer treated for decades with hormone drugs, redrawing that distinction could redirect both research and second-line treatment choices.
plos-pone-0011575:
Maria Jesus Garcia, Maria Carmen Nuñez, and Robert Ashley Cox used theory in 2010 to sharpen a routine lab measurement in a mycobacterium. Ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, are built from RNA and protein parts made at rates a growing cell must coordinate. The team measured the synthesis rates of three ribosomal components in Mycobacterium fortuitum, a fast-growing relative of the tuberculosis germ.

Because the standard test, qRT-PCR, carries known biases, they built a theoretical approach to design and read the experiment more honestly. Clocking how fast a germ builds its protein factories reveals its growth strategy and its vulnerabilities, since many antibiotics attack ribosome construction. The theoretical care matters as much as the numbers: synthesis rates computed naively can be wrong by design. The paper gives microbiologists both the rates and a cleaner way to obtain such rates elsewhere.
plos-pone-0011675:
Delphine Peric and co-authors studied cells from a patient with a rare sugar-processing disorder, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells build sugar chains on a carrier called dolichol inside a compartment named the ER, as a first step in coating proteins with sugars. The work starts on one face of the compartment and continues after the chain flips inside.

In cells from a patient with the disorder CDG Ig, the team tracked free sugar chains carrying phosphate tags. Their locations revealed a previously unknown route moving material from the ER back to the cell body. That hidden traffic helps explain the disorder's tangled symptoms.
plos-pone-0011775:
Ruth Peters and co-authors modelled mental decline in very old patients with high blood pressure, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Thinking skills tend to slip with age, but in older adults the process is fluid and can move in stages. High blood pressure is tied to faster decline, yet whether treating it changes the path was unsure.

With data from the HYVET trial, the team modelled how thinking changed and built risk tables proposed for wider use. Those tables help doctors spot the patients whose minds are slipping fastest. Better forecasts support earlier help for the old patients at greatest risk.
plos-pone-0011875:
Michelle Kiebala and colleagues found in 2010 a natural brake on inflammation linked to HIV infection in the brain. HIV's Tat protein can drive production of TNF-alpha, an inflammatory signal tied to the cognitive problems grouped as HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder. The team studied RelB, a member of the NF-kappa B family of gene switches.

RelB held back the TNF-alpha production that Tat sets off. That is notable because other members of the same family usually push inflammation forward. A built-in counterweight inside the same switch family suggests the body already owns part of the machinery needed to limit this harm, if researchers can learn how to favor it.
plos-pone-0011975:
Seth Egger, Heidi Engelhardt, and Kenneth Britten measured in 2010 how quickly monkeys correct their steering using vision. The brain circuits behind primate navigation are largely unknown, and progress needs direct tests of how movement is guided. Steering is a clean case: the eyes see drift, and the hands or body must respond.

Monkey steering responses revealed rapid visual-motor feedback, corrections arriving faster than a deliberate reaction would allow. Speed like that implies dedicated, near-automatic loops between eye and movement systems. Knowing the true delay in the loop constrains any model of how primates move through cluttered ground without stumbling.
plos-pone-0012075:
Shuai Lu and co-workers aimed in 2010 to tag embryonic stem cells with glowing nanoparticles that find their target. Tagging stem cells would help scientists follow them for development studies and for regenerative medicine. Nanoparticles had already proven to be a sturdy platform for delivering genes and imaging cells without invasive steps.

The team conjugated peptides, short protein pieces that act as address labels, to quantum dots, then used them to target embryonic stem cells. Addressed dots that home to stem cells could light them up inside a living body. That visibility is what stem cell therapy needs before anyone can prove the cells go where they are sent.
plos-pone-0012175:
Lasse Sinkkonen, Tabea Hugenschmidt, Witold Filipowicz, and co-authors looked for a gene-silencing machine at the cell's protein factories, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Small RNAs guide silencing machines that shut genes off, and parts of that machinery also turn up near chromosomes, where they shape which regions stay active. Whether such a machine sits at the DNA that builds ribosomes, the cell's protein factories, was an open question.

They found Dicer, a core silencing protein, associated with that ribosomal DNA in mammalian cells. The ribosome supply line is one of the most guarded places in the genome, since growth depends on it. A silencing role there would link two systems, gene control and growth control, that textbooks usually keep apart.
plos-pone-0012275:
Lina Thors, Anders Bergh, Emma Persson, and co-authors measured a cannabis-system enzyme in prostate cancer tissue, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The body's own cannabis-like signals are broken down by an enzyme called FAAH, and signs pointed to this system going off balance in cancer. Using a well-characterized bank of patient tissue samples, they measured the enzyme against the cancer's receptor levels, severity, and patient outcomes.

They also tested how an immune signal regulates the enzyme. Links between this enzyme and how aggressive a tumor proves could make it both a prognostic marker and a drug target, since blockers of it already exist in development for pain. Reusing such compounds against cancer is an attractive shortcut.
plos-pone-0012375:
Louise Harewood, Monica Liu, Jean Keeling and colleagues reviewed forty-five cases of babies born with both kidneys missing or badly underformed, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The condition, shortened to BRAHD, is a common lethal birth defect. Known risk factors include diabetes in the mother, yet most cases have no clear cause, leaving families without answers.

Alongside the case review, the team mapped the breakpoints of two new chromosome swaps found in patients, pinpointing where the DNA broke. Each mapped break narrows the search for genes that build the kidneys. The combined case data and gene clues give doctors a firmer base for counseling families and guiding future research.
plos-pone-0012475:
Mouli Das, Subhasis Mukhopadhyay and Rajat De applied a classic optimization trick to gene networks, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Gene regulatory networks — who switches whom on or off — underlie development and disease, and their wiring is hard to infer from data. The authors borrowed gradient descent, the hill-climbing method used to fit models, and aimed it at network pathways.

Their method tunes network models step by step toward matching measured gene behavior. A working inference method lets biologists move from lists of genes to working maps of control. Such maps are the starting point for predicting how a cell will react to a drug or a mutation.
plos-pone-0012575:
Charles Francis, Alex Borisenko, Natalia Ivanova and colleagues applied DNA barcoding to Southeast Asia's mammals, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The region is one of Earth's biodiversity hotspots, and habitat loss puts much of it at risk, yet even the basic inventory of mammal species is incomplete. A short standard DNA stretch can identify species quickly, if reference libraries exist.

The team showed barcodes can reveal hidden diversity, flagging look-alike populations that are likely separate species. Correct names and counts are the foundation of conservation law and funding. Barcode libraries built now become the baseline against which future losses in the region are measured.
plos-pone-0012675:
Diaz-Ferguson, Haney, Wares and co-authors read the genes of a sea snail to map how Caribbean life connects. Rocky shore animals are classic models for how larvae drift between coasts. Their 2010 study focused on a trochid gastropod, a top-shell snail spread across the region.

Gene patterns showed how strongly snail populations exchange members across the sea. That exchange decides whether a protected area can restock its neighbours. Their wider map of Caribbean links helps planners place marine reserves where currents and larvae actually travel. Their snail serves as one clear case among many.
plos-pone-0333775:
Jr Nyambi Nkiackmenyi Ramin and colleagues measured cadmium, a toxic metal in cigarette smoke, among healthy smokers in Buea, Cameroon. Smoke carries many poisons together, so liver and kidney harm cannot be pinned on one metal alone. One hundred and two smokers were grouped as light, moderate, or heavy, with blood and urine tests for liver and kidney markers, set beside non smokers.

Cadmium per gram of tobacco was similar across major brands. Heavy smokers breathed in many times the safe daily level, though their share of weekly tolerable intake stayed in single digits. Liver and kidney markers ran worse in smokers, and rose with smoking load. Cutting smoking, the authors stress, cuts a proven multi poison exposure.
plos-pone-0334375:
Ryadul Alam and colleagues worked with teenage girls at four schools in Savar, near Dhaka in Bangladesh, during early 2025. Their survey asked what the girls knew about breast cancer and whether they ever checked their own breasts for lumps. Nearly four hundred students took part, drawn from different class levels at each school.

Knowledge was low overall, at about one third of the best possible score. Fewer than half had even heard of self checking, and only a tiny share had ever tried it. Girls in science classes and girls from families with higher incomes knew more. Knowing more also went hand in hand with actually doing the checks, which points to a clear need for school teaching.
plos-pone-0337675:
Ana Quiroz-Huanca and colleagues sped up a DNA test for a gene that helps E. coli resist a vital family of antibiotics. Their method pairs a faster version of standard DNA copying with a CRISPR-based step that glows when the resistance gene is found. Speeding the heating and cooling cycles cut the copying stage from eighty minutes to about half an hour.

The full check finished in under an hour and still detected mere handfuls of bacteria in spiked poultry droppings, a realistic farm sample. A version using a locally made enzyme took slightly longer but also worked. Because the workflow needs only basic lab equipment and modest skill, the authors pitch it for smaller laboratories that now wait days for resistance answers.
plos-pone-0341275:
Nikita Bhattarai, Sunil Kumar Joshi, and co-authors studied road traffic injuries among undergraduate students who ride two-wheelers in Nepal's Kathmandu district, where motorbikes dominate and injuries are climbing. Their 2026 mixed-methods study surveyed more than twelve hundred students across four colleges and interviewed five stakeholders for remedies.

Nearly one student in four reported a traffic injury during 2021 and 2022, most often bruises to arms and legs. Only about seventy-eight percent held a driving license. Injuries cost students class time and strained family budgets through medical bills and repairs. Stakeholders produced five headline recommendations, which the authors present as a practical agenda for making student riding safer in a rapidly motorizing country.
plos-pone-0342975:
Wrestlers may fight several bouts in one day, and tired thigh muscles can unbalance the knee. Ali Tatlıcı and colleagues measured front and back thigh strength in sixteen young national-level wrestlers, at rest and after fatigue, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Two ratios were tracked: a standard one comparing peak strengths, and a functional one matching the muscles as they actually work together during movement. Machine tests measured squeezing and lengthening contractions in both states. The team examined which ratio better reflects risk when athletes are tired, since injuries cluster late in tournaments. Findings should guide conditioning that protects knees across a long competition day.
plos-pone-0346175:
Awoun Jung and Izumi Uehara present this 2026 PLOS One study of how Japanese preschoolers learn to read emotions. Ninety children aged three to six took part. They completed tasks on reading others' minds, on mental flexibility and memory, and on vocabulary. They also took tasks on reading emotions. The question was how these skills hang together while language grows so fast.

All three skills linked to reading emotions. Language stood at the center. Once vocabulary was counted, the link between reading minds and reading emotions vanished. That link runs through language. Mental flexibility kept both a direct link and one through language. The authors argue that boosting language growth may be a practical lever for young children's emotional growth.
plos-pone-0346675:
Luciano Gristina, Ettore Barone, and Riccardo Scalenghe measured soil loss in a super-high-density olive orchard on a Sicilian slope, where trees are planted as machine-harvested hedgerows. Such intensive orchards are spreading across the Mediterranean, but their erosion cost on semi-arid hillsides was undocumented. The team combined carbon-isotope soil profiles, erosion pins, and satellite vegetation data over the orchard's six years.

The hedgerow orchard lost soil at a rate rivalling vineyards and far above traditional olive groves. Bare ground between rows covered nearly two-thirds of the surface, and downhill tillage carved channels. The authors recommend permanent cover crops, mulch, and contour working to keep intensive olives from washing the hillside away.
plos-pone-0347675:
Yaru Dang and four colleagues published this 2026 supply chain study of a cash-strapped retailer borrowing against its inventory. A supplier sets wholesale prices while a bank designs the loan, choosing interest rates and how much of the stock value it will advance. The authors modeled how these choices push on each other and where safe advance limits sit.

When the retailer borrows to the limit, the supplier prices at the highest workable level and the bank charges its highest workable rate. Mid-range advance rates often beat the maximum. Dang maps when inventory financing truly pays.
plos-pone-0347775:
Yuanyuan Hu improves a learning method that teaches driving robots to navigate by sight. Such robots can misread their surroundings and react too slowly. The 2026 paper upgrades a classic trial-and-error algorithm with sharper gradient guidance, aiming for more accurate and faster visual navigation in complex settings.

In tests, the improved method reached high accuracy and beat comparison approaches. Its success rate in simulated driving rose well above that of traditional methods. In real-world runs, the robot made navigation decisions about a fifth faster. Quicker, steadier sight-based steering could widen where self-driving machines can safely work, from warehouses to roads.
plos-pone-0347875:
James Laurence and Emer Smyth followed more than two thousand Irish teenagers through the pandemic years to see which hardships left a mark on wellbeing after schools reopened. Ireland endured especially long closures. Survey waves from before, during, and after the crisis let the team separate passing distress from damage that stuck, across education, family life, friendships, and household money.

Some stressors that hurt at the time, such as health anxiety and struggling with home learning support, faded without a trace. Others lingered: frayed family and friend relationships, especially for girls, household money shocks, heavy screen time, and having no quiet place to study. Money shocks and screen time harmed later wellbeing directly, not just through misery at the time. The authors argue recovery support should target these specific scars.
plos-pone-0347975:
Hossain and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Bangladesh, test a urine marker that could flag diabetic kidney damage earlier than the standard test. The standard urine albumin test often wakes up late, after the kidney's filtering cells, called podocytes, are already hurt. Podocalyxin is a protein shed from those cells into urine, so it may rise sooner.

Eighty-eight adults took part: people with type 2 diabetes sorted by albumin level, plus healthy controls. The new marker climbed step by step from healthy people through the diabetes groups, and it tracked closely with the standard test and with blood sugar control. Set at the right cut points, it sorted the groups with high accuracy, even telling healthy people from diabetic patients whose albumin was still normal. The authors present it as an early warning candidate, to be confirmed in larger, longer studies.
plos-pone-0348075:
Ratana Saipanish and her team built a scale for a soft but strong trait: how folk rate their own inner stores. These stores hold traits like kind hearts, bend-apt minds, duty, and clear thought. No tool had aimed at this self view head on. The team drafted the scale with Thai pros and group talks. Five hundred fourteen Thai grown-ups then took the draft.

The scale was cut to twenty-five items in four groups. It held up with high marks for trust. High scores sat with grit, self worth, and good mood. Low scores sat with low mood and worry. The team gives the scale to wards and labs that study growth of the self.
plos-pone-0348175:
Sara Trbojevic and colleagues catalogued the cells of rat jaw joint cartilage, healthy and arthritic, one cell at a time. The jaw joint is unusual: its cartilage descends from a different embryonic source than other joints and has a layered structure. Using single-cell RNA sequencing on a rat model of jaw osteoarthritis, the 2026 study traced which cell types live there and how they change in disease.

Cartilage-building cells split into several fates growing out of shared ancestors, and a growth factor called pleiotrophin marked a progenitor population in the proliferative zone. In diseased cartilage, support cells reacted to inflammation while cartilage cells burned energy on repair, and cell-to-cell chatter intensified. The atlas guides future jaw joint therapies.
plos-pone-0348275:
Julia Braun and co-workers test a simple fitness check used with people who stay ill long after COVID-19. The check counts how many times a person can stand up from a chair and sit back down in thirty seconds. Their 2026 paper draws on data from a treatment trial with one hundred fifty adults to judge whether the test is safe, steady, and useful.

No one was harmed doing the test, and scores were fairly steady when repeated about two weeks apart. Still, repeat scores varied enough that a real change must be fairly large to trust. Scores linked only weakly with daily activity and with key symptoms. Nearly half the group scored below the lowest normal range, showing how deep the loss of function can run.
plos-pone-0348575:
Andrew Hughes and co-workers estimate how much life people in England actually lost to COVID-19, accounting for how frail each person already was. Debate swirled over whether those who died were near death anyway. Their 2026 study links health records for the whole registered population and simulates each infected person's survival with and without the infection.

For people over sixty-five who died, the middle estimate of life lost ran close to five years. More than a quarter would likely have lived at least five more years without the infection. Younger-old women showed the strongest such share. The results rebut the claim that pandemic deaths mostly replaced imminent ones, and the method could run live in future outbreaks.
plos-pone-0348675:
Protyoi Chakraborty and co-authors used computer chemistry to examine two of the world's most common painkillers, ketoprofen and ibuprofen, together with the breakdown products they leave behind. Their 2026 study is entirely computational. It models each molecule's structure and energy, predicts how the compounds bind to a key inflammation enzyme, and screens them for harmful effects.

Some breakdown products bound the target enzyme more strongly than the parent drugs, while others showed warning signs for cancer risk, kidney harm, and blood toxicity in the prediction tools. Simulated complexes stayed stable over a long virtual run. The authors argue that drug residues and their leftovers deserve more attention as a health and environmental concern.
plos-pone-0348775:
Ivy Meihua Su, Keyu Li, and Winsy Wing Sze Wong set out a plan for a review of dementia care studies. Many care homes use group work such as music, chat, and games. These can lift mood and calm stress. But one thing is rarely checked: how much do the people with dementia join in, and does joining in change how well the work helps?

The team will search five big databases for studies that gauged this joining in. They will list the tools each study used. They will also check if any study linked those scores to health gains. This is a plan, not a set of results. Its aim is a shared way to gauge engagement in dementia care.
plos-pone-0348875:
Rafael Mauti and colleagues compared two walking tests for spotting older adults at high risk of falling. One test mixes walking with a second task at the same time. The other, the Walking Trail Making Test, weaves the thinking task into the walk itself, like following a trail of targets. One hundred one community-dwelling older people took both tests and were classed by an official screening tool.

The built-in trail test, in its hardest version, separated high-risk walkers more accurately than the add-on dual-task walk. Dual-task tests let people cheat by prioritizing one task, which muddies results. Falls are a leading cause of injury in old age, so a sharper screening test helps target prevention where it counts most.
plos-pone-0348975:
Elizabeth McCarthy and colleagues asked whether cannabidiol, the non-intoxicating cannabis compound, can protect the eyes of diabetic fish. Zebrafish kept in sugary water for four weeks developed high blood sugar, weak responses to moving patterns, and faulty electrical signals from the retina, mirroring early diabetic eye damage. Some fish received the compound in their water throughout the sugar exposure.

Treated fish performed better on the vision behaviour test, though their blood sugar stayed just as high, separating protection from glucose control. Electrical responses improved only partly, with some timing delays appearing instead, and a key barrier protein in the retina still fell. The authors conclude the compound softens some visual harm without fixing the underlying damage, a mixed result that argues for cautious, deeper study.
plos-pone-0349175:
Xinjian Li and co-authors trained a hybrid vision model to outline cracks and water leaks on tunnel linings. Inspectors miss damage under poor light and rough surfaces, and simple threshold software fails there too. Their 2026 framework, TransUNet, marries convolutional networks, which read local texture, with transformers, which track long shapes across an image.

The training set mixed public benchmarks with real engineering photographs, all prepared through one pipeline. Against leading rivals, the hybrid scored best on crack outlining, reaching a solid overlap score. Thin, blurred defects and boundary detail improved most. Li and colleagues propose the system for routine tunnel health monitoring, where early cracks and leaks are cheapest to fix.
plos-pone-0349375:
Changhwan Sung and colleagues taught a neural network to imagine the late brain scan used in Parkinson's diagnosis from an early scan alone. The tracer involved binds the dopamine transporters that vanish as the disease progresses, but the clearest pictures come hours after injection. Their system learned from nearly five hundred paired scans to generate the delayed image from the early one.

Generated images matched real ones closely, and the standard binding scores computed from them correlated strongly in both an internal check and a fresh set from a different scanner type. Diagnostic accuracy for spotting abnormality held up in one set but slipped in the independent one, a gap the authors report plainly. If matured, the method could shorten scan visits for frail patients.
plos-pone-0349575:
Sarah W Feldstein Ewing and colleagues lay out a trial plan, with no results yet, on peer help during group counselling for young drinkers. The trial will enrol about two hundred and fifty adults aged eighteen and nineteen who report recent binge drinking. Pairs will take part in group motivational interviewing, a talk method that builds a persons own reasons to change.

While pairs talk, both brains will be scanned at the same time so the team can measure how closely their activity lines up. Focus falls on kind, pro health words aimed at a peer. Later drinking will be tracked to see whether brain alignment during peer support links with real cuts in alcohol use.
plos-pone-0349675:
Aliakbar Mariki and colleagues tested liver fluke secretions in mice with chemical damage to nerve insulation, a stand in for multiple sclerosis. The human disease joins immune attack with slow loss of insulation around nerves, and current drugs rarely fix both. Mice got fluke products during the damage phase, with movement, memory, inflammation markers, and insulation proteins tracked.

Treated mice showed lower inflammation markers, higher insulation protein levels, better preserved insulation staining, and stronger movement and memory scores than untreated damaged mice, though not full recovery. Parasite products that calm the immune system may inspire a new class of nerve protecting drugs, with much safety work ahead.
plos-pone-0349775:
Uma Shashi Sharma, Philip R LeDuc, and Yongjie Jessica Zhang built a framework in 2026 for sorting the shapes of dendritic spines, the tiny knobs where brain cells receive signals. Spine shape tracks learning and development, but analysis choices are usually fixed in advance without testing.

Their framework tries many shape reduction and grouping methods side by side on microscope data, then scores how well the layouts preserve known relations between spine types. A second data set from different imaging conditions tested generalisation. Some method pairings kept the biology legible while others scrambled it. The comparison itself is the contribution, guiding labs away from flattering but misleading maps.
plos-pone-0349875:
Hongtao Zhang, Yang Liu, and Junbo Yan studied square concrete filled steel tubes under pulling loads in 2026. Such members brace tall structures, and predicting their strength from few tests is a standing problem for engineers.

A detailed computer model was checked against six physical specimens, then varied to test size, confinement, and slenderness effects. Strength rose steeply as confinement grew and fell as slenderness increased. National code formulas landed close to the model, the Chinese code closest. A generative network was then used to stretch the small data set for machine learning prediction, a practical trick where tests are expensive.
plos-pone-0350075:
Han Wu and five colleagues examine which training habits go with injuries among keen recreational runners, in this 2026 survey of parkrun participants in the UK. Parkrun's free weekly races draw millions, and many chase personal bests. From more than five hundred performance-minded runners, the team gathered a year of training and injury history, then analyzed it with both classic statistics and machine learning.

Contrary to common belief, strength and conditioning work did not come with fewer injuries; resistance training and stretching or yoga were actually linked to slightly more injuries. Machine learning echoed the stretching result, added a benefit for frequent interval sessions, and found runners guided by qualified coaches fared better. The authors caution that injured runners may take up such exercises because they are hurt, but the findings challenge easy assumptions about injury prevention.
plos-pone-0350175:
Afschin Gandjour authored this 2026 PLOS One modeling study weighing the European Union's tougher medical device rules against deaths in Germany. The regulation promised safer devices, but certification bottlenecks and product withdrawals may have cost lives by making devices unavailable. Gandjour combined a population-level elasticity method with a device-by-device accounting under clearly stated assumptions.

Official German reports count very few device-related deaths each year, while international estimates run far higher, and the model's withdrawal and delay effects ranged widely depending on which baseline was used. Under central assumptions, the long-term safety gains outweigh the harms, but transition-period losses could be substantial, especially for niche and children's devices. The author recommends targeted fixes to protect those categories.
plos-pone-0350275:
Brandon Chongthanadon and co-authors reviewed the economics of reversing sterilisation in 2026. Some people who chose vasectomy or tubal sterilisation later want children, and the choice between reconnection surgery and assisted conception is partly a money question.

Searching three databases up to late 2025, the team found twenty-four cost studies, almost all from rich countries. Thirteen covered tubal repair and eleven vasectomy reversal, each weighed against fertility treatment. Reporting quality was checked against a standard list, and costs were converted to one year's dollars. The review gives clinics and patients a cleaner basis for a decision often made under time pressure.
plos-pone-0350575:
Pengfei Qu, Lei Song, and Sihan Wang blend physics with learning to predict concrete strength and design mixes that meet strength targets reliably, even with little data. A physics based starting formula uses water, binder, and age, then a small neural net learns only what physics misses, keeping results sensible and monotone where they should be.

On a public set of over one thousand mixes, the hybrid scored high accuracy and held up when trained on only forty percent of data. Checks confirmed age and cement help strength while water hurts, as physics expects. Honest uncertainty bands covered the promised share of cases. Builders can design greener mixes with less cement and known risk.
plos-pone-0350675:
Ai-Hsien Adams Li and colleagues reopened a nineteen nineties experiment on using light-activated drugs to keep reopened arteries from clogging again, and reported it with unusual candor. In rabbits with balloon-injured leg arteries, one side received photodynamic therapy with the drug porfimer sodium and the other served as control. Scar-like growth inside the artery was measured three weeks later.

The therapy worked biologically: treated arteries showed marked suppression of the unwanted growth. But the procedure killed four of ten rabbits during surgery, and complications left only three animals with usable paired samples. That gap between efficacy and feasibility is exactly why the approach stalled decades ago. The reappraisal preserves a cautionary dataset modern device teams would otherwise never see, failures included.
plos-pone-0351075:
Sara Cromer and three colleagues examine this 2026 PLOS One study of whether better income and education protect against diabetes and obesity equally across American racial and ethnic groups. Using two large datasets, a national examination survey and the All of Us cohort, they modeled disease rates by education and income within each group.

Higher education and income were clearly tied to lower diabetes and obesity rates among White and Asian participants. Among several other groups, including Black participants, the protective link was smaller or even reversed, and the patterns took different shapes depending on the measure used. The authors warn that risk calculators which fold in social measures can mislead unless such differences between groups are checked.
plos-pone-0351675:
Coralie Goetz and seven colleagues hunt for natural weapons against bacterial biofilms in this 2026 study. Biofilms are slimy fortresses that shield bacteria from antibiotics. They drive stubborn infections, including mastitis in dairy cows. Earlier work by the group found something intriguing. Four mild staphylococcus strains, themselves weak biofilm builders, suppressed biofilm growth in most mastitis-causing staphylococci they met.

Fluid from those friendly strains carried the protective effect. It even reduced later colonisation by the dangerous Staphylococcus aureus in a mouse mastitis model. Nobody yet knew which molecules did the work. This study sets out to isolate and characterise them. The four producer strains span two species from cow udders. Finding defined antibiofilm compounds could seed new treatments that disarm infections without relying on conventional antibiotics, a pressing need as resistance spreads.
plos-pone-0351775:
Laís Carneiro and five colleagues ask invasion scientists which harms of invasive species matter most, in this 2026 survey of more than four hundred experts worldwide. Invasions damage ecosystems in many ways, and managers cannot fight every harm at once. The experts rated nineteen types of ecological impact across habitats, kinds of organisms, and levels from single populations to whole communities.

Clear patterns emerged. Changes to community structure, shrinking populations, and outright species loss were judged most important. Effects on soundscapes, fire patterns, and microclimate consistently scored lowest. Ratings varied more across kinds of organisms than across habitats, and seasoned experts agreed with each other more closely. The authors suggest the top-rated impacts deserve management priority, while the low-rated ones may reflect gaps in knowledge that research should close.
plos-pone-0351875:
Xianhong Huang and six colleagues examine what makes local clinics ready for emergencies. Their 2026 survey covers primary healthcare institutions in China. Nearly one thousand health professionals answered questionnaires. The team modelled how emergency readiness connects with workplace culture. They also weighed the trust, networks, and shared understanding an institution can draw on.

Workplace culture was linked to stronger emergency capacity. So were all three forms of social capital: structural, relational, and cognitive. Culture also worked partly through social capital, which carried its influence onward. Community type changed the recipe. In ordinary communities, relationships mattered most. In older communities, formal network structure carried more weight. Clinic leaders therefore need both inner culture-building and outer relationship work, tuned to the neighbourhood they serve.
plos-pone-0352075:
Aravind Krishnan and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on lung cancer screening data. It harmonizes the National Lung Screening Trial, a landmark study whose CT scans came from many scanners. Harmonizing here means correcting for two scanner settings, field of view and the reconstruction kernel's resolution, which change how images look.

Without such compensation, differences between machines masquerade as differences between patients' lungs. A harmonized trial dataset lets later researchers, including AI teams, pool scans honestly. Imaging scientists reusing this famous dataset for new studies are the audience for careful correction work.
plos-pone-0352275:
Nagham Faris and four colleagues chart emergency department traffic at a Beirut hospital through the pandemic's lockdown era. Their 2026 retrospective study uses administrative records from February 2020 to April 2022. Nearly seventy thousand patients passed through, about a fifth of them children. Lebanon's experience matters because most published lockdown research comes from wealthy countries. Volumes and diagnoses were compared between the lockdown and post-lockdown periods.

After lockdown, the patient mix grew younger. Children's share of visits jumped from about seventeen to twenty-four percent. The authors read that surge as a catch-up effect: postponed care arriving late. Adult volumes, by contrast, recovered slowly. Paediatric visits for respiratory infections, COVID-19, and ear diseases all spiked. Emergency planners in lower-income settings now have local evidence that reopening brings a child-heavy wave, not a simple return to the old normal.
plos-pone-0352575:
Yu Wen leads a team of six stress testing waste rock slopes inside a cold region coal mine, in PLOS ONE in 2026. At the Chaoyang open pit in Heilongjiang, dumped spoil slopes must survive soaking rain, deep frost, and seeping groundwater. The team squeezed and sheared spoil samples at four moisture levels and three temperatures, from warm room conditions to deep subzero. Then they fed the measured strengths into a three dimensional slope model. They also checked drainage in the field.

Water was the enemy at ordinary temperatures: wetter spoil grew weaker and the computed safety margin slid steadily. Freezing reversed the risk, since ice binding the pores stiffened the material and rain barely dented safety. Drainage pipes delivered the practical win. They lifted the safety factor substantially before and after simulated rain. The study gives cold climate mines a season aware playbook for dangerous piles.
plos-pone-0352675:
Huawei Zhi and Yan Qiao study in 2026 how emotions spread online around health topics before and after officials correct a rumour. They gathered interaction data from a large Chinese platform and treated official corrections as key turning points. Analysis combined feeling scores, network structure, and a method that looks at which mixes of conditions occur together.

Before correction, topic type stirred positive feeling in careful readers, while big voices stirred it in followers. Dense networks with big voices could also spread negative feeling fast. Corrections helped most when a topic was already widespread and audience values aligned. Popularity alone did not guarantee a better mood.
plos-pone-0352875:
Lu, Lee, and Yoon reviewed studies on video game competition and thinking skills in a 2026 paper. Competitive gaming demands fast attention and quick decisions, but proof of lasting mental effects is mixed. Nine studies met the review's rules, drawn from two major databases.

Most studies compared skilled and less skilled players at one point in time. A few tested training, single-session play, or lifestyle factors like sleep and load. Themes covered skill-level differences, health habits, and how decisions are made in play. The thin and varied evidence base means strong claims about gaming sharpening the mind are premature, a useful caution for schools and teams.
plos-pone-0352975:
Seyong Chang and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One air quality study mapping fine particle pollution across greater Athens, Greece, at a fine one-kilometer scale. Ground monitors are sparse, so the team combined monitor records from 2007 to 2019 with satellite data, weather, and land-use information, and stacked three machine learning methods into an ensemble.

The ensemble reconstructed daily pollution levels accurately across the city and years. Average particle levels sat above both World Health Organization and European limits, peaked in the earliest year studied, and rose each mid-winter, likely from home heating and trapped air. The authors say such maps let researchers estimate what residents actually breathe in places monitors never reach.
plos-pone-0353175:
Nurullah Çelik, Ceren Bolat, and Ahmet Dönmez present this 2026 PLOS One experiment on whether table tennis sharpens attention and careful decision making. Twenty-eight sports science students took part; half enrolled in an elective table tennis course and half did not, with groups assigned at random. Everyone completed an attention test and a decision-making questionnaire before and after the course period.

Scores for concentration and careful decision making rose in both groups over time, and the rise reached statistical significance as a general time effect. However, the table tennis group did not improve significantly more than the control group. The authors conclude that the sport may support these skills but that larger studies are needed before claiming a clear training effect.
plos-pone-0353275:
Ademe Mihiretu, Melaku Asresu, and Kindye Ayen report this 2026 PLOS One farming study on spreading an improved field pea package in Ethiopia's dry Waghimra zone. Over four seasons, more than one hundred selected farmers grew the new variety and methods on shared clusters of land, even though the approach contradicted local habits. Researchers tracked yields, how fully farmers adopted the package, and whether the seed spread further.

The improved package out-yielded local practice by roughly seventy percent. Most farmers applied the full package with expert support, and nearly all wanted to keep growing it, even though many found it labor-heavy. Participants also passed seed to neighbors, spreading the variety beyond the trial. The authors recommend seed cooperatives and stronger partnerships to scale the approach across similar dry areas.
plos-pone-0353375:
Kifelew and colleagues field-tested spring wheat lines against a major leaf disease in Ethiopia in a 2026 study. Forty-five lines grew under natural infection at a research center over two seasons. Disease was scored by damaged leaf area and by density of the fungus's fruiting specks.

Six lines resisted well, holding up even against strains that defeat several major resistance genes. Heavier disease cut plant height, seed number, and grain yield in clear patterns. Genotype drove over two-fifths of the difference in disease levels. Resistant lines like these give Ethiopian breeders ready material for crosses that protect harvests without heavy spraying.
plos-pone-0353475:
Julian Cortes and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study building a heart-risk score designed specifically for people with psoriasis. Psoriasis involves body-wide inflammation and raises the risk of heart and blood-vessel disease, but standard risk tools were built for the general public. The team used records from the All of Us research program to find which factors best predicted serious cardiovascular events in these patients.

Their score combines age, sex, blood pressure, and diabetes with a new marker built from routine blood counts of neutrophils, platelets, and monocytes. It placed patients in low, medium, or high risk bands, and event rates differed sharply across them over ten years. The authors suggest it could flag psoriasis patients who need closer heart monitoring using tests clinics already run.
plos-pone-0353675:
Yu Wang and six colleagues mine a large United States hospital database for what drives sepsis after ovarian cancer surgery, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, is among the most dangerous complications after major operations. Records for nearly forty thousand patients treated between 2010 and 2019 were compared according to whether sepsis followed their surgery.

About one patient in thirty developed sepsis, and the rate crept up over the decade. Those patients stayed longer, cost more, and died in hospital more often. Heart failure, clotting problems, and spread of the cancer beforehand raised the risk. Knowing the warning profile helps surgical teams watch the right patients hardest.
plos-pone-0353775:
Svenja Hehn and three co-authors redesign a workhorse enzyme so it can copy RNA at higher temperatures, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The enzyme, borrowed from the T7 virus, manufactures the synthetic messenger RNA used in research and modern vaccines. Hotter reactions make less of a harmful double-stranded by-product, but the natural enzyme wilts in the heat.

Using a design tool that compared four crystal structures of the enzyme, they combined the shared suggested changes into new variants. One kept working at a temperature where the natural enzyme failed, and produced clean RNA with no detectable by-product. Heat-tolerant copying could make vaccine-grade RNA purer and simpler to produce.
plos-pone-0353875:
Ulrich Frey and Atul Pokharel ask why some farmer-run irrigation systems in Nepal keep working for decades while others fail, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Cross-sectional snapshots cannot answer that, so they built a rare long-term record covering more than two hundred community systems. Each system was revisited sixteen to thirty-seven years after its first survey.

Machine learning models pointed to a consistent pattern. Systems did best when outside help was available but leaders were themselves water users. Fair rules, regular member meetings, and occasional outside assistance predicted survival. Good day-to-day organisation, more than physical design, seems to decide whether shared irrigation endures.
plos-pone-0353975:
Mevlüt Sinan Ocak, Mehmet Eskibağlar, and Mustafa Gündoğar compare ways of sealing root canals in teeth from patients with diabetes, in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. Diabetes changes dentine, the tooth layer fillings must grip. Forty extracted single-root teeth were filled by four techniques: two traditional packing methods with a resin sealer, and two newer approaches built around a ceramic sealer.

Slices of each root were then pushed against until the filling gave way. The ceramic-sealer methods bonded significantly more strongly, especially in the middle and tip sections of the root, while the two traditional methods tied with each other. For diabetic patients, the authors suggest, modern ceramic sealers may hold root fillings more securely.
plos-pone-0354175:
Zhichen Ling, Xinlei Ren, and Bingquan Luo published this 2026 study of why some football clubs' official statements after Champions League matches grab heavy media attention while others sink. They selected twenty-five club-event cases across six seasons and scored media visibility alongside response delay, shock of the result, match stakes, and how far the message strayed from the club's template.
