Attention followed combinations, not single causes: one steady route paired quick, calm replies to big matches with legacy-flavored wording. Ling warns against blaming speed or strategy alone for publicity outcomes.
plos-pone-0354275:
Allison F Lewis, Rachel Bohnenkamp, and Jill Campbell Stewart published this 2026 study of how genes shape learning from praise. Fifty-two adults practiced a joystick sequence task over two days, getting either plain timing feedback or timing plus flattering social comparison. Saliva DNA grouped them by how strongly their dopamine system tends to run.

Praise helped learners with average dopamine profiles but not those in the low group, whose retention lagged under comparison. High-group learners improved either way. Lewis suggests pep-talk feedback is not one-size-fits-all, and genetics may decide who benefits.
plos-pone-0354375:
Jiang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, dissect nearly five hundred accidents at refined oil depots in China to find the paths that lead to disaster. Depots store and move huge amounts of flammable fuel, so spills can become fires and explosions. The team cleaned official records and mapped how causes connect to each other, not just which causes are common.

Most accidents happened in storage areas and during loading and unloading. Spills were the most common event, and human operational errors the most prominent single cause. Network analysis then traced four critical pathways, and every one ran through operational errors, fed by weak training or poor procedures, sometimes via equipment defects. Protection defects also ranked as critical. The practical message is sharp: train people and write better procedures first, since the road to a depot fire usually starts with a person, not a pipe.
plos-pone-0354475:
Lodha and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how living arrangements shape binge drinking in teenage mice. The teen years bring sensation seeking and weak brakes on risky acts, and being cut off from peers can warp brain development. The team housed young mice alone, next to neighbors, or in groups, then offered alcohol.

In one drinking test, housing made little difference as mice grew into early adulthood. In a second test that models binge drinking in the dark phase, mice housed alone drank more, in both sexes. Group-housed mice given alcohol at the same time drank much less than isolated ones. Adding more bottles raised how much a cage drank overall but did not erase the gap between group and single housing. Teen binge drinking raised adult intake only in group-housed mice. The authors read this as social context steering the urge to drink, in both directions.
plos-pone-0354675:
Xiangxin Liu led a team of six authors on this 2026 wireless engineering paper for future 6G networks. A promising signal format survives fast movement well but wastes power when signal peaks spike. Their scheme masks the signal and rebuilds it at the receiver with a physics-informed neural network that sees the whole frame at once.

The network, shaped by classic signal theory rather than blind layer stacking, corrected errors better than standard deep models while using fewer parameters. Liu notes hardware and over-the-air tests must come before claiming real deployment readiness.
plos-pone-0354875:
Jaweria Jalil Awan, Muhammad Hamid, and Tagrid Alshalali build a hate speech detector for Roman Urdu in this 2026 paper. Roman Urdu, the language written in Latin letters, is widespread online but lacks the labeled data and fixed spelling that automated moderation tools rely on. Their model mixes a large multilingual language model with attention layers and, crucially, a hand-built lexicon of abusive Roman Urdu terms.

The lexicon does double duty, guiding what the model pays attention to during training. Tested on a dataset of thirty thousand posts, the system classified hate speech with accuracy near eighty-nine percent. Follow-up experiments showed the lexicon guidance genuinely helped with tricky spellings, negations, and informal variations. The work brings automated protection to a language community that big platforms largely overlook.
plos-pone-0354975:
Chunjie Li and four colleagues published this 2026 simulation study of highway speed limits in rainy weather. Rain cuts tire grip and shortens what drivers can see, and hills make both worse. Their model blends road friction, slope, and sight distance into safe speeds, plus a car-following model tuned for wet driving, tested on a real highway near Hangzhou.

Simulated speeds matched observed traffic closely, and the strategy cut conflict rates steeply under heavier rain. Gentle rain needed no extra limits, while a downhill grade proved the riskiest layout. Li offers the results for adaptive rainy-day speed control.
plos-pone-0355275:
Julia Fa and colleagues interview in 2026 hunters, cooks, and sellers along the wild meat trade in rural Cameroon to map disease risk from handling animals. Thousands of structured talks covered villages and regional markets. Wild meat feeds many families and earns income, yet contact with animal fluids can pass infections to people.

Hunting and handling habits varied by ethnic group, gender, and age, with one Indigenous group more likely to hunt bats, a high risk animal. Almost nobody used protective gear, few cleaned surfaces with soap, and many ate or sold meat from visibly sick animals. Worry about disease was low, though worry did raise safer habits a bit.
plos-pone-0355375:
Jobin K and colleagues compared two school yoga programs for teenagers in India. One was a standard government yoga protocol. The other wove in mindfulness meditation. Their 2026 study assigned 147 secondary students to one of the two programs or a waiting list. Both programs ran for twenty-one days. The team measured distress, mindfulness, and emotion control. It also measured well-being before, after, and three months later.

Both yoga groups improved over the control group. The mindful version produced bigger gains in mindfulness and healthy reframing of emotions. It also lifted well-being more and cut distress more deeply. Its edge held at follow-up. The standard protocol's benefits were smaller and faded faster. The study suggests the mental training ingredient, not just the postures, carries much of yoga's school value.
plos-pone-0355475:
Kentaro Ito and co-authors report in 2026 a small crossover trial in healthy men on a coated form of medium chain fat. The coating used milk protein around tiny fat particles, meant to aid uptake in the gut. Each man took both the coated and plain forms on separate occasions, in random order and without knowing which.

Blood ketones over six hours did not differ overall between the two forms. Peak levels of ketones and of a key fatty acid were still higher after the coated form, and stomach effects stayed mild for both. The authors suggest the coating may sharpen the early response without adding harm.
plos-pone-0355675:
Patricia Moreno-Peral and colleagues published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on a digital program meant to prevent depression before it starts. An earlier doctor-delivered version, predictD, already prevented depression and anxiety in Spanish primary care. The new e-predictD version adds an app, a validated risk calculator, and decision support. Each patient gets a personal prevention plan drawn from eight modules covering exercise, sleep, problem-solving, relationships, and thinking habits.

Six family doctors in six cities enrolled fifty-six patients without depression, all at moderate to high risk, and most completed the pilot. Patients and doctors discussed the plan in a short first visit, chose modules together, and used the app between visits. Satisfaction, usability, and acceptability were mainly tested, using interviews plus standard mood, anxiety, and quality-of-life questionnaires. This small, control-free pilot is treated as a design check ahead of a full trial.
plos-pone-0355975:
Xiaojing Wu and colleagues study a gene helper called ILF3 and its role in making red blood cells, with a focus on beta thalassemia. People with that inherited blood disorder cannot make enough healthy red cells. Their 2026 paper combines single-cell gene data from patients and healthy donors with a lab experiment that switched the gene off in blood cells.

Patient cells carried less ILF3 than healthy cells, and cells that kept it looked more mature and active in growth pathways. Cells without it showed stress and inflammation signals instead, and red cell growth seemed to stall early. Switching the gene off also pushed lab cells toward early death. Wu and co-authors suggest that losing ILF3 helps explain the failed blood production in this disease.
plos-pone-0356175:
Mohamad Radwan Sirri and four colleagues review the harms side of a tempting dental offer in this 2026 paper: surgery to speed up orthodontic tooth movement. Cutting the bone around teeth can shorten treatment, but moving teeth always risks eating away their roots, and surgery might make that worse. The review gathered eleven comparative studies covering just over three hundred fifty patients, focusing specifically on measured root loss.

Evidence certainty was low to very low throughout. Simple bone-cutting procedures showed either small increases in root loss or no clear difference from standard braces, while some graft-assisted techniques measured slightly less loss than controls. Observed damage generally stayed within accepted clinical limits, but the studies were small and inconsistent. The authors say a large added risk is not demonstrated, yet firm safety conclusions are not yet possible.
plos-pone-0356275:
Hege Kersten and six others publish a protocol in 2026 for a Norwegian registry study on medication use just before a dementia diagnosis. People developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia usually carry other illnesses and take many drugs; some of those drugs are a poor fit and can worsen thinking. What happens in the year before diagnosis, when symptoms are starting but unnamed, has not been described in Norway's clinics.

The planned study links three national registries covering thinking assessments, dispensed drugs, and hospital records for everyone diagnosed in such clinics over a decade. It will estimate how common heavy medication use and risky prescribing were in that pre-diagnostic year, and which patient traits accompany them. The authors hope the map will guide safer prescribing and well-targeted efforts to trim needless drugs.
plos-pone-0356375:
I. M. Shindy and six colleagues propose a simpler way to keep electricity protection working in microgrids, in this 2026 engineering paper. When a small grid adds its own generators, fault currents grow and change direction, which can confuse the overcurrent relays that isolate faults and can overstress breakers. One remedy is a device placed between the microgrid and the main network that limits fault current in a chosen direction.

The challenge is sizing that device's resistance correctly. Instead of running heavy optimization, the authors derive it directly from a standard equivalent-circuit measure of the network, a pencil-and-paper style calculation suited to real-time engineering use. Tests across scenarios with conventional generators, wind turbines, and solar panels showed the method restored relay coordination and curbed fault currents without new relays or adaptive schemes.
plos-pone-0356475:
Zheng Li and colleagues graded the groundwater beneath the main urban area of Bozhou City in Anhui Province, China, using two independent mathematical methods that check each other. Their 2026 study combined a projection technique that lets the data itself set each measure's importance with a second method built to handle the fuzzy borders between water quality grades.

Both approaches placed the city's groundwater at the second-best grade, with closely matching scores, and stress tests confirmed the verdict was stable. Agreement matters because grading methods often smuggle in subjective weights, leaving results easy to challenge. A verified grade gives local managers a firmer basis for deciding where drinking water protection and pollution control should focus.
plos-pone-0356775:
Caner Mavili and colleagues split forty-five young male basketball players into faster and slower groups. The split used a curved sprint test around the three-point arc. The team then compared jumping and strength profiles to find what separates the groups. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured drop jumps, countermovement jumps, and an isometric pull. Dozens of force and timing metrics came from each test.

The fast group's advantage lived in quick force. It showed shorter ground contact and stronger braking and takeoff in the drop jump. It showed stronger braking in the countermovement jump. Force development in the pull was far faster, even though peak pull strength did not differ. One rapid-force measure at a split-second window matched curved sprint contact times almost exactly. Coaches chasing change-of-direction speed should train explosiveness, not just strength.
plos-pone-0356875:
Hamid Ali Khan and coauthors published a 2026 field study in PLOS ONE on wheat breeding for the dry north of Pakistan. Yields there have stagnated for two decades as local varieties share a narrow gene pool. At a university research farm in Peshawar, they grew twelve Chinese hybrid wheat lines beside two local cultivars across two growing seasons, recording emergence, tillering, grain weight, and final yields.

Two hybrid lines clearly outperformed the rest. They sprouted early, produced the most tillers and spikes, carried the heaviest grains, and out-yielded the leading local cultivar by roughly a sixth. Statistical analysis confirmed wide genetic diversity among the hybrids, and yield rose together with its component traits, which helps breeders select efficiently. The authors recommend the two leading lines as parents and candidates for northern Pakistan's semiarid farms, arguing that fresh hybrid germplasm can break the long yield plateau.
plos-pone-0357275:
Cai Xu, Juehyun Shin, and Graciela Muniz-Terrera study whether social isolation tracks with overall healthy aging capacity among older Hispanic adults across the United States. Capacity here bundles movement, senses, thinking, mood, and energy into one score. Using a national retirement survey from a recent year, the team analyzed several hundred adults aged sixty and over, then probed rural, community, and birthplace subgroups.

Across the whole group, isolation showed no clear link with capacity. Inside subgroups, though, patterns surfaced: isolated rural elders scored lower, as did isolated United States-born elders, while higher income and fewer chronic diseases tracked with higher capacity nearly everywhere. Xu and colleagues call the subgroup results exploratory and ask for longer studies before programs lean on them.
plos-pone-0357375:
Marjorie Vázquez-Roldán and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on breast cancer screening among older women in Puerto Rico. They linked the island's central cancer registry with health insurance records to study women aged fifty and older who had been diagnosed with breast cancer. The team asked whether living with anxiety or a mood disorder changed how likely women were to get mammograms, be diagnosed late, or die within five years.

Among more than four thousand women, those with anxiety or a mood disorder were actually more likely to have had a recent mammogram than women without such diagnoses. Yet that extra screening did not lead to earlier-stage diagnoses, and it did not change five-year survival. The authors say screening programs should look beyond mammograms alone, and they call for more work on severe mental illness and cancer detection.
plos-pone-0357475:
Bailey Lankford and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on pollinator hotels, the drilled blocks and tubes people install for cavity-nesting bees and wasps. The title calls such hotels parasite hideouts, flagging a risk in a popular conservation habit.

The authors focus on preserving native cavity-nesting Hymenoptera, the bees and wasps themselves, through better pollinator hotel management. Hotels that shelter parasites as well as pollinators can backfire, so management details matter. Gardeners, land managers, and pollinator advocates are the readers who need to know how to keep these shelters helpful.
plos-pone-0357575:
Hidetaka Onda and colleagues build a simple score to flag patients likely to return to the emergency department within a day of going home. Very early returns can signal a missed problem, but most discharge data tools aim at longer windows. Using records from one hospital's discharges in a recent year, two doctors hand-checked which returns were unplanned, and the team searched routine visit data for warning signs.

Only a small share of patients returned within a day. Five simple items made the final score: arriving without an ambulance plus four blood test patterns tied to inflammation and red cell traits. Each added point raised the odds of return. Onda and colleagues present the score as decision support, not a verdict, for busy discharge moments.
plos-pone-0357975:
Kathryn Malherbe, Carol A Benn, and Gerhard Botha evaluated AI support for breast ultrasound across several sites, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The system, called Breast AI, helps sort patients by risk during breast cancer assessment. Many AI tools are tested only in labs; this evaluation ran inside real clinical pathways.

Malherbe's multi-site observational work shows whether the AI helps clinics judge risk accurately under daily pressure. Real-world testing matters because lighting, workflow, and patient mix vary by site. If support holds up across sites, assessment can move faster without losing care. The study also gives other clinics a model for checking AI in their own pathways before adopting it.
plos-pone-0358075:
Carina Liebl leads a team of seven reading the geology inside Bronze Age rock carvings in Bohuslän, Sweden, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The granite panels, a world heritage treasure, carry ships, people, and animals pecked into the rock. The team combined ultrasound scans of the stone's interior with three dimensional surface models at five panels, asking whether carving depth follows the rock's structure rather than the carver's strength.

Sound revealed two weak, fracture rich layers a few millimeters down, relics of glacial stress relief. Nearly every figure sat within the first weak layer, averaging about a millimeter deep, deeper than the weathered crust but never reaching sound stone. A nearby polished but uncarved outcrop lacked the layered weakness entirely. The conclusion flatters the ancient carvers: they chose panels the geology had pre softened, and placed figures where the stone would yield, practical knowledge earned from the rock itself.
plos-pone-0358275:
Dandan Liu, Huixia Ji, Ye Chen, and Tongzhou Zhou published a 2026 health study in PLOS ONE linking years of factory noise to fatty liver in male car-plant workers. Fatty liver tied to metabolic dysfunction is a whole-body disorder, and noise may disturb metabolism through stress pathways, not just hearing. They examined several hundred noise-exposed men by ultrasound and tested whether body weight changed the noise relationship.

Just over half the workers had fatty liver on ultrasound, and longer noise exposure went with higher likelihood overall. The pattern depended on weight, though: among normal-weight men, each extra year of noise exposure raised the likelihood noticeably, while in overweight and obese men the added effect was not statistically clear. Their baseline risk was already high. Hearing-conservation programs, they say, should treat long noise exposure as a metabolic risk too, especially for lean workers who look low-risk.
plos-pone-0358475:
Xinyi Qiu, Limei Guan, and Hui Liu analyzed diabetes in teenagers worldwide, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Diabetes is striking younger, with effects on schooling, growth, and lifelong health. Using data from a major worldwide study of disease burden, in its 2023 round, the team tracked the burden among teenagers across more than three decades and projected future trends.

Qiu's analysis shows how unevenly that burden is shared across countries, and where it is rising fastest. Forecasts give health systems warning of what is coming, from clinic load to insulin demand. Teenage onset means decades of living with the disease, so early trends carry outsized costs. Solid global numbers help argue for prevention aimed at the young.
plos-pone-0358575:
Saeed Ghasempour leads a team of six adapting a measure of patient centered communication for Iranian nurses, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nurses are patients' primary human contact in hospitals, and how centered their communication is can now be scored by an existing scale. No version had been tested outside its home country. Three hundred clinical nurses in Shahroud hospitals, in two independent samples, answered the Persian translation while specialists reviewed every item for cultural and conceptual fit.

The expert panel deleted one item whose meaning duplicated another. Statistical work then proceeded in stages: exploratory analysis to find the scale's structure, confirmatory analysis to test whether that structure holds, and consistency checks within and across time. The study is methodological groundwork. Once a translated instrument survives this gauntlet, Iranian hospitals can benchmark communication, compare units, and judge training honestly. Without it, patient centeredness stays a slogan nobody can measure.
plos-pone-0358775:
Esther M Choo leads a team of eight studying how caregivers and health workers received a home nutrition screening program in western Kenya, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The Family MUAC approach teaches parents to measure a child's upper arm with a simple tape to catch wasting early, backed by two way text messages with health workers. An earlier trial found the approach cut child wasting by more than a third; this study asked why people engaged with it.

Through eight focus groups and interviews with caregivers and staff from three facilities, the team found the program rated acceptable, workable, and empowering, and families felt it saved them money. Uptake among caregivers was high. Participants also suggested folding growth checks into other routine health services to sustain the habit. The accounts explain the trial's success in human terms and point to how such programs spread.
plos-pone-0358875:
Jeon Mi Lee and three colleagues revisit how hearing aids are fitted for people who wear one in a single ear, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Clinics can verify a fitting by measuring sound right at the eardrum, or they can start from the maker's automatic settings and fine tune by feel. Robin, Turck, Hainard, and co-authors present pROC, an open-source package for analysing and comparing ROC curves. ROC curves are useful tools for judging classifiers, such as diagnostic tests, in biomedical and bioinformatics work. Conclusions drawn from them are often reached through inconsistent or thin statistics, though.

The package supports researchers with proper methods to plot curves, measure accuracy, and test whether two curves truly differ. It runs in both R and S+ environments. Sound curve analysis helps teams avoid overstating a test's power to separate disease from health.  Benchmarks in the paper show the package running fast on ordinary hardware.
pmc-3937975:
Kweon, Kim, Jang, and co-authors profile KNHANES, short for Korea's National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. This national surveillance system has assessed how healthy and well nourished Koreans are since 1998. It operates under the National Health Promotion Act.

The surveys are conducted by the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. They combine interviews, health examinations, and nutrition assessment on a representative sample. A data resource profile like this one tells researchers worldwide what the survey holds and how its long record can track national health change. Its records support studies of diet, chronic disease, and ageing across decades.
pmc-4792175:
Wilkinson, Dumontier, Aalbersberg, and many colleagues set out the FAIR Guiding Principles in 2016. They argue there is an urgent need to improve how scholarly data are managed and reused. Stakeholders from academia, industry, funders, and publishers came together to design the principles.

FAIR stands for data that are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable. The principles are concise and measurable, so groups can check whether they meet them. Most research data were being lost or locked in forms machines could not use. FAIR became the global reference for data stewardship, shaping funder rules and repository design ever since.
pmc-4987875:
Trifinopoulos, Nguyen, von Haeseler, and their team presented W-IQ-TREE in 2016. IQ-TREE is efficient software for phylogenetic analysis by maximum likelihood, a method that finds the evolutionary tree that best explains sequence data. Many users, though, prefer a web tool over command lines.

W-IQ-TREE puts IQ-TREE on the web behind a simple, friendly interface. It supports multiple sequence types, including DNA, protein, codon, and morphology data, in common alignment formats. Fast tree building on the web opens serious analysis to smaller teams. Such trees underpin studies of species history, virus spread, and gene evolution.
pmc-5431875:
Bhardwaj, Kaur, Wuest, and their co-authors reported in 2017 on making cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors by in situ click chemistry. Cyclooxygenase-2, or COX-2, is a promising anti-inflammatory drug target. Too much of this enzyme also shows up in several cancers and in diseases that destroy nerve cells.

A challenge is selectivity: the inducible COX-2 is very similar in sequence and structure to the housekeeping COX-1, which the body needs. In situ click chemistry lets the enzyme itself assemble its own inhibitor from small building blocks inside its binding site. That approach can yield selective compounds that design alone might miss. The work offers a route to safer anti-inflammatory and possibly anticancer agents.
pmc-5651175:
The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network produced this study of esophageal cancer in 2017. Cancers of the esophagus are common worldwide, yet few targeted drugs exist and survival stays poor. The team ran a full molecular workup on tumors taken from patients in both Western and Eastern countries.

Their results split esophageal cancers into distinct groups with different genetic patterns. One group looked much like stomach cancer, while another matched head and neck cancers more closely. That split matters because it suggests the groups may need different treatments. The work gives drug developers a clearer map of what to target in each type.
pmc-5824275:
Tomi Akinyemiju and many Global Burden of Disease colleagues reported the burden of primary liver cancer in 2017. Liver cancer is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Its main causes include hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and alcohol use.

The study gives global, regional, and national figures for cases and deaths from 1990 to 2015. It breaks the totals down by cause so trends stand out. Hepatitis-linked cancer fell in some places as vaccines and treatment spread, while other causes grew. Health leaders use these numbers to target prevention where it will save the most lives.
pmc-6415775:
Christopher Stewart, Nadim Ajami, Jennifer O'Brien, and colleagues charted the early gut microbiome in the TEDDY study in 2018. TEDDY follows children at raised genetic risk for type 1 diabetes. Gut microbes and immunity shape each other strongly in the first years of life.

Sampling stools from infancy onward, the team maps how the gut community assembles. Feeding mode, antibiotics, and siblings all leave marks on that path. The study sets a baseline for later tests of whether microbial patterns forecast diabetes. Its scale makes it a reference for child microbiome research.
pmc-6550175:
Alvin Rajkomar, Eyal Oren, Kai Chen, and coauthors tested deep learning on electronic health records in 2018. Hospital records hold rich clues about patient outcomes. Hand-built prediction models use only a small, curated slice of that data.

Feeding raw records from two hospitals into deep networks, the team predicted death, readmission, and length of stay. Their models beat standard tools without manual variable crafting. The work showed one data format could serve many tasks at scale. It also raised lasting questions about bias, explanation, and safe use at the bedside.
pmc-6607375:
Stefan Elbe and Gemma Buckland-Merrett examined GISAID and virus data sharing in 2017. Sharing virus data fast is critical when a lethal outbreak starts. Scientists need sequences to judge the threat and build countermeasures.

GISAID was created to coax influenza data into the open by crediting those who share. The authors explain how its access rules and trust building overcame hoarding. Governments also gain tracing power from shared data. The model later proved central during the coronavirus pandemic, when sequence sharing through GISAID shaped global tracking. The analysis draws lessons for sharing data on other fast-moving health threats as well.
pmc-6786975:
Clare Bycroft, Colin Freeman, Desislava Petkova, and coauthors described the UK Biobank resource in 2018. The project recruited about half a million adults across the United Kingdom in midlife. It pairs deep health records with genetic data at unmatched scale.

Measures span lifestyle, blood tests, imaging, and linked hospital records, all open to bona fide researchers. Rich phenotyping lets one cohort serve studies of heart disease, brain aging, and much more. The paper is the standard citation for the resource. Its openness set a template that newer national biobanks now copy.
pmc-6973275:
Jack Bowden and Michael Holmes reviewed meta-analysis within Mendelian randomization in 2019. The randomization method uses genes as instruments to test causal effects. Meta-analysis, in turn, combines results across studies.

Early randomization studies each used few genetic variants, and pooling was simple. Modern studies use hundreds of variants from huge samples, which changes what pooling means. The review sorts the old and new senses of combining and warns where each misleads. It clarifies language that much of the causal inference field now shares. Notation and worked examples keep the discussion usable for readers new to either method.
pmc-7260975:
Jian Shang and co-authors explained in 2020 how SARS-CoV-2, the virus behind COVID-19, breaks into human cells. Both this virus and the earlier SARS virus use the human ACE2 protein as their entry receptor. They also rely on human enzymes, called proteases, to activate the viral spike before entry can happen.

The team compared the two viruses side by side using lab made copies of the virus and standard biochemical tests. From those experiments they picked out the exact features of entry that set the newer virus apart, including how firmly its spike grips the receptor. Knowing the doorway and the key in this detail points drug makers toward the steps most worth blocking.
pmc-7681775:
Monika Litviňuková and colleagues cataloged in 2020 the cell types that make up the healthy adult human heart. Heart disease kills more people than any other condition, yet the full roster of cells in a healthy heart, and what each type does, was still incomplete. The team profiled cells from different regions of the heart to fill that gap.

Their atlas describes the muscle cells, vessel lining cells, support cells, and immune cells found in each chamber and region. It also shows how gene activity varies between them, and how the mix of cells differs across the heart. A reference map of the healthy organ gives disease researchers the baseline they need to spot exactly which cells go wrong.
pmc-7778975:
Kevin Howe and a large team of collaborators reported in 2020 the state of Ensembl, a genome browser and data resource focused on vertebrate species. Ensembl annotates genomes, marking where genes sit, how they are structured, and which elements regulate them. It also traces how genes evolved across species, so a finding in one animal can be compared with its counterpart in another.

The report describes the annotation work and data releases current at the time, and how the project shares them freely with the world. Ensembl is a daily tool for geneticists studying everything from human disease variants to wildlife conservation. This account shows the scale of the quiet work needed to keep genome data usable.
pmc-7857475: In 2026, a team published An applied paradigm for simple analysis of the l. The work broke new ground. Time has kept the file intact through the years. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
rink-tales-traditions-eskimo-1875:
Hinrich Rink spent years in Greenland as a Danish official, and this set of tales came out in 1875. He gathered the tales from Inuit tellers in their own land. The book brought Greenland's oral lore to English readers on a large scale for the first time. Rink had the tales writ down in the tongue in which they were told.

The tales tell of hunts, spirits, ghosts, and the deeds of old heroes. Many show the angakok, the shaman, at work between men and hidden powers. Rink kept the voice of the tellers close, so the book reads as Greenland speaking for itself.
rockefeller-commission-report-1975:
A presidential panel judged the CIA's acts at home in June 1975 and found much to blame. The Rockefeller Commission report tells of mail opened, of the CHAOS files on war foes, and of MKULTRA drug tests. Nelson Rockefeller chaired the panel for President Ford.

The report prints the facts of the abuse and the laws it broke, in the government's own words. One part, on the killing of foreign chiefs, was cut by the White House before the book came out. The gap is noted in the file and in the lore of the age. The volume marks the first great public reckoning with the agency.
saint-martin-des-erreurs-1775:
Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin published Des Erreurs et de la Vérité, On Errors and Truth, in 1775. He signed it only as the Unknown Philosopher, the name that followed him for life. The book is the founding text of Martinism, his own theosophic teaching, and it carried that current into French high-degree Masonry.

Saint-Martin argues that man's fall explains both nature's order and its wounds. True knowledge, he holds, repairs the mind's errors one by one. His prose is dense, earnest, and visionary. The French esoteric revival begins on these pages. Later Martinist orders traced their charter to this first book of the philosopher who hid his name.
sargent-proof-palpable-immortality-1875:
Epes Sargent claims the dead can be touched in The Proof Palpable of Immortality, his book of 1875. Forms that took shape in the dark room are his theme. Hands were grasped, faces seen, and weights and prints taken by fans who swore the forms were not the seer in dress or mask.

Sargent prints their sworn tales in dense rows. He holds such proof ends all doubt on life past death. Foes found fraud in case past case since then. The book is the high tide mark of that strange wave of faith.
spurgeon-lectures-to-my-students-1875:
Spurgeon's Lectures to My Students, published in 1875, gather his Friday talks to the men of his Pastors' College in London. The college trained working men for the Baptist ministry without charging fees. The lectures cover preaching from call to delivery.

Spurgeon advises on voice, gesture, sermon choice, prayer, and the pastor's own temptations and sorrows. His wit is famous: whole pages read like stand-up comedy with a theological point underneath. Generations of preachers have called the book the wittiest work on homiletics, the art of preaching, ever written. Students treasured the talks enough to print them for a wider world.
stewart-tait-unseen-universe-1875:
Balfour Stewart and P. G. Tait were two Scots men of science of high rank. Their Unseen Universe came out in 1875 with no names on it at first. They argue that laws of heat and force point to a world past sight. That world, they hold, holds the soul's life to come.

Heat must run down, they grant, and the stars must cool in time. Yet force is never lost, they say, but flows to an unseen realm. Faith and lab facts meet in a bold, strange blend. The book was a hit and stirred years of talk on science and faith.
swedenborg-earths-in-the-universe-1875:
Emanuel Swedenborg first wrote of the earths in the sky in 1758. The dress here is the English one of 1875. Its full old title speaks of the earths in our solar scheme. Swedenborg said spirits from those worlds spoke with him for years.

Moon folk, Mars folk, and the rest pass in a long chain of tales. Each race has its own bent of mind and way of faith. Swedenborg links their traits to the parts of one grand man in heaven. The book is the root text of the faith view of peopled worlds.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume twenty-five of Casanova's memoirs: late adventures of the rover. The wanderer's road winds on. Autumn of the great lover. Twenty-fifth volume: autumn of the lover, late adventures, autumn of the great lover.
the-phantom-of-the-opera-pg175: Leroux's 1910 Phantom of the Opera haunts Paris with Erik's masked love. Chandeliers fall. The Tower library holds the full text. It sang below. Masks hid. thomas-erceldoune-prophecies-murray-1875:
Thomas of Erceldoune, called Thomas the Rhymer, was a Scots seer and poet of the 13th century. James A. H. Murray edited his romance and forecasts for the Early English Text Society in 1875. The text gives the old Scots words with full notes.

The romance tells how Thomas met the Queen of Elfland and got the gift of true speech. The forecasts that bear his name deal with kings, wars, and the fate of Scotland. Murray's edition is the full record of a lore that Scots quoted for ages. The old Scots text is given with care and full gloss.

Rudolf Steiner gave the lectures behind Christianity as Mystical Fact in the early 1900s, before his later spiritual movement took full shape. He reads Christianity as the flowering of the ancient mystery religions of Egypt and Greece. The life of Christ, for Steiner, is a cosmic event, not only a historical one.

Symbols, rites, and initiation practices from the older mysteries are traced forward into the Gospels. Steiner argues the mysteries prepared humanity for what Christianity revealed openly. Dense at times, the lectures launched his lifelong spiritual philosophy and show the point where his thought about religion, history, and hidden knowledge began to join together.
tob-10175:
Micah prophesied in the 700s BC, and his book is the thirty-third in this King James ordering. A prophet from outside the capital, he spoke against corrupt rulers, dishonest merchants, and hollow worship. His language is plain and furious, aimed at people who used religion to cover injustice.

His most famous line asks what God requires: to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God. Elsewhere the book looks toward a ruler from Bethlehem and a time when nations beat swords into plowshares. Judgment and hope stand side by side, and the hope is for ordinary people as much as kings.
tob-10375:
Ralph Shirley lined up a gallery of occultists and mystics from many periods, sketching lives, claims, and followings. Astrologers, alchemists, and seers pass in review. Shirley writes as a curious observer of the borderlands of belief rather than as a disciple of any one figure.

Each sketch treats its subject as a window on what an age believed possible: hidden forces, secret knowledge, second sight. Some figures are famous, others nearly forgotten, and the tone stays entertaining rather than credulous. Readers get a compact tour of occult reputations across history, useful as a starting map before deeper studies of any single tradition.
tob-13329-15475:
Books four to seven, in volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata, carry the Pandavas from hiding back to open war. A year in disguise at a foreign court ends in revelation and alliance. Krishna's peace mission to the Kauravas fails against pride and envy.

Then Kurukshetra's eighteen days begin in earnest. The Bhagavad Gita stands at the center, Krishna's teaching to a warrior who cannot bear to fight his kin. Armies clash, vows are kept at terrible price, and heroes fall daily. Ganguli's prose rises to the scale of the fighting. The epic's blazing middle is all here.
tob-14475:
C. W. Leadbeater mapped the astral plane in his 1895 Theosophical manual, describing the realm of emotion and desire said to lie just beyond the physical world. Scenery, inhabitants, and phenomena receive systematic treatment. The traveler in sleep, the recently dead, and various non-human beings all have assigned places in his geography.

Leadbeater wrote as a clairvoyant investigator reporting a country, complete with its dangers and its uses for students. Concise and orderly, the manual became the Theosophical movement's standard guidebook to the unseen, shaping how occultists pictured the afterlife and dreams for decades. Readers can judge his calm, cataloging tone against the strangeness of the territory claimed.
tob-4075:
Michal Sedziwój, the Polish alchemist known as Michael Sendivogius, published A New Light of Alchymie in 1604, drawn, by its title, from the fountain of nature and manual experience. His treatise gives nature its own confession: all metals grow in the earth from a central life force, and the adept can learn its ways by study and experiment.

Sendivogius writes alchemy at its most philosophical, arguing about air, seed, and the hidden food of life in terms later chemists would echo in new vocabularies. Isaac Newton annotated Sendivogius closely, one sign of his reach. Among alchemical texts, few influenced the coming chemistry as directly as this Polish courtier's dialogues.
tob-4146-15475:
Exile ends in volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata, which covers books four through seven of the Sanskrit epic. The Pandavas come out of hiding, demand their share of the kingdom, and send Krishna as a peace envoy to the Kaurava court. The mission fails, and both sides gather huge armies.

Then the eighteen-day war of Kurukshetra begins. At its heart stands the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's counsel to the warrior Arjuna, who shrinks from killing kin. Battle follows counsel: duels, slaughters, and falls of famous heroes crowd the pages. Ganguli keeps the vast cast and carnage clear, and the tragedy lands with full weight.
tob-9052-15475:
Volume two of Ganguli's Mahabharata brings the Pandavas out of exile to claim their rights. Krishna himself carries their peace terms to the Kaurava court, speaks with courtesy, and is refused with contempt. Both sides then muster armies drawn from half the kings of India.

On the field of Kurukshetra the slaughter begins. The Bhagavad Gita sounds at the battle's heart, as Krishna steadies Arjuna for the fight. Days of duels and massed charges follow, with famous warriors falling in turn. Ganguli's Victorian prose keeps the huge action clear. The peace has failed; the epic's terrible center has begun.
treaty-of-orleans-1275:
The Treaty of Orléans of 1275 joins England and France in this record. The pact belongs to the reign of Edward I of England. Medieval kings settle their cross-Channel claims in formal, sworn terms.

Homage is rendered, disputes are compromised, and peace is sworn. Two great crowns of Christendom compose their quarrel for a season. The forms are solemn: seals, oaths, and kinship ties bind the deal. Thirteenth-century statecraft shows its formal face in the treaty's clauses. Short truces like this one paved the road to longer wars between the crowns. The record's sparse detail leaves the pact's exact terms to the clauses themselves.
un-ga-res-52-175:
Guatemala's peace moved into its next phase under Resolution 52/175, passed by the General Assembly in 1998. The UN Verification Mission in Guatemala had its mandate stretched to 31 March 1998 by a vote of March 1997. A July 1997 text had urged all sides to push ahead with the second phase of the peace plan, which ran to the end of that year.

The text weighs the mission's seventh report on human rights. It also weighs a report on the strides made by Central American lands in peace, freedom, and growth. The Secretary-General's counsel on the mission's work is before the Assembly: how to shape it so it can meet the needs of the peace check in full.
un-ga-res-a-69-75: Young diplomats learn the trade of disarmament through a UN training plan backed in Resolution A/69/75, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The programme of fellowships on disarmament dates to the first special session on the subject. The text notes that the plan still builds grasp of why disarmament counts, and of the worries states bring to the table. A large corps of trained officials, from many lands, has passed through it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 52/175 was adopted on 18 December 1997. It keeps the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala, known as MINUGUA, working through the third full year after the country's peace accords were signed. The short resolution reviews how the long civil war settlement is holding up, including reports by the Secretary-General and Guatemala's own peace commission.

The Assembly renews the mission for 1 April to 31 December 1998. It asks the Secretary-General to keep reporting. It asks him to recommend how the mission should continue after that. It thanks Guatemala's government, its former insurgent movement, and donor countries for backing the process. The renewal mattered because a standing United Nations presence was the main outside guarantee that the 1996 peace accords would actually be carried out.

Adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, resolution 69/75 of the General Assembly reviews the United Nations disarmament fellowship, training and advisory services, then in their thirty-sixth year. It thanks China, Germany, Japan, Kazakhstan and Switzerland for hosting study visits in 2013 and 2014. It asks the Secretary-General to keep running the programme each year within existing resources. The programme trains officials from member states in arms control and disarmament.
un-sc-res-1375: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 1375, catalogued here for 2001. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1475:
A detailed Cyprus settlement plan failed at The Hague in March 2003. The Secretary-General and his adviser had worked on it since 1999. On 14 April 2003 the Security Council praised that extraordinary effort. The plan of 26 February 2003 was balanced with care, the Council said. It gave the text its full support as a rare chance for a deal. The plan aimed to bridge decades of division on the island.

The Council regretted how the talks had ended. It blamed the negative approach of the Turkish Cypriot leader. His stance at The Hague blocked a vote on the plan. Both communities were meant to decide in referenda. A year later a revised plan did reach a vote, and the sides split.
un-sc-res-1575: Under its sequence number 1575, a formal Security Council decision is preserved in official-record form. English Wikisource supplied the transcription held here. The text's two-part shape does the work: recitals justify, operative clauses command or request. For anyone tracing what the Council required at a given moment, that primary wording is the evidence.
un-sc-res-1675:
Western Sahara's mission was renewed in the spring of 2006. On 28 April 2006 the Security Council extended MINURSO until 31 October 2006. The Secretary-General had reported on the territory days earlier. The Council restated its promise to help the parties find a settlement. That settlement must be just, lasting, and accepted by both sides. It must also let the territory's people choose their future.

The military agreements behind the ceasefire had to be respected in full. Member states were asked to fund family visits for divided Sahrawi families. Such visits were the main trust-building step on offer. The Secretary-General owed a report before the term ended. His zero-tolerance rules on abuse also applied to the mission.
un-sc-res-1775: Resolution 1775, adopted in 2007, is preserved in this collection as a Security Council decision in record form. Its record notes a December 31 adoption, the Council working to the year's last day. The text itself follows the standard pattern, and the entry keeps it whole through the Wikisource transcription of the official record.
un-sc-res-1875:
UNDOF's mandate ran through another renewal in June 2009. On 23 June 2009 the Security Council extended the Golan force until 31 December 2009. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission that month. The conduct clause took its now-standard place in the text. UNDOF had to enforce the zero-tolerance policy on abuse. Its personnel had to meet the United Nations code of conduct.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 at once. A report was due at the end of the term. It would cover events in the area and steps toward 338. The force's observers kept their posts along the separation line. The renewal passed without debate, as most UNDOF texts do.
un-sc-res-275:
Portuguese attacks on Guinea's villages drew the Council's anger in 1969. Guinea had sent three letters detailing the raids. Forces based in Portuguese Guinea-Bissau had caused heavy damage. On 22 December 1969 the Council deplored the loss of life and the harm done. It said such incidents endanger world peace. No state, it added, may act against the Charter's principles.

Portugal had to stop violating Guinea's sovereignty and borders at once. Its authorities had to free a captured Guinean civilian plane and its pilots. They also had to release a seized motor barge, the Patrice Lumumba, with its passengers. Both seizures dated from 1968 and 1969. Six members abstained, but the text passed.
un-sc-res-675:
Central America's observer group won six more months in November 1990. On 5 November 1990 the Security Council extended ONUCA until 7 May 1991. The Secretary-General's October report received approval. The group watched the region's peace agreements from its 1989 mandate. Nicaragua's civil war had ended in elections that year. Demobilization of fighters was the mission's core task.

The Council noted the need to watch spending with care. Demands on peacekeeping funds were growing fast in 1990. The extension kept observers in place across five countries. Their reports helped confirm that the peace accords held. ONUCA was among the first missions of the post-Cold War wave.
un-sc-res-75: Who pays for the helpers of UN field teams? Security Council Resolution 75, passed on 27 September 1949, takes up that small but real cost. A 1948 Assembly vote had left it to the Council to rule if a team member needs a deputy at his side. Where that need is found, the UN may pay back the travel and daily costs of such deputies, for time past as well. The text lists the teams whose members had each needed such help, from the Good Offices team in Indonesia on.
un-sc-res-975:
Haiti's security handover from the multinational force to the United Nations was set in motion on 30 January 1995. The United States-led force had declared a secure and stable environment in place. The former military leaders had left, and the elected president had returned. Haiti's own letter of 27 January supported the transfer.

The Council found the conditions of resolution 940 (1994) for ending the multinational force were met. It authorized the Secretary-General to prepare for the United Nations Mission in Haiti, UNMIH, to take over the force's functions. He would work with the force commander on the steps needed. States that had served in the multinational force won the Council's thanks, as did the Organization of American States and its civilian mission. UNMIH's mandate was extended to 31 July 1995, at up to 6,000 troops and 900 civilian police.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Burundi's peace process, and a transitional government taking shape, win the Council's backing on 29 October 2001. The Arusha Peace and Reconciliation Agreement of August 2000 remained, in the Council's view, the best basis for ending the conflict. A summit in Pretoria had just agreed the new government's framework and membership.

Armed groups, the FDD and the FNL, were called on to stop attacks on civilians, end the fighting, and join the talks. The Council strongly backed an interim multinational security presence, requested by Burundi's government and led by South Africa, to protect returning exiles and train an all-Burundian protection force. Donors were urged to fund relief, the return of refugees, and rebuilding.

A grand plan to heal Cyprus died at The Hague in March 2003. The UN chief had built the plan since 1999. He had honed it twice, in December 2002 and in February 2003. Votes in both halves of the isle were to seal it. The Turkish Cypriot chief balked at the last meet, on 10 and 11 March. Resolution 1475 passed with no dissent on 14 April 2003.

The Council voiced its deep regret. A chance to vote on a shared land had been lost. Greek and Turkish Cypriots alike had been denied their say. Faith in the chief's plan stayed firm. It was named the sole base for fresh talks. His good offices stood open. All sides were urged back to the table to forge a full deal on its lines.

Bosnia and Herzegovina's peacekeeping changes hands in this text of 22 November 2004. The NATO-led SFOR was ending its mission, and a European Union force was set to succeed it in December. Full support is restated for the High Representative and for carrying out the 1995 peace agreement.

Acting under Chapter VII, states working through the European Union are authorized to run the stabilization force for a further planned period. Those states may take all necessary measures to carry out the peace agreement's military terms and to defend the force. The parties are told to respect the force's safety and freedom of movement, and reporting to the Council will continue.

Trinidad and Tobago entered the United Nations through Resolution 175, adopted unanimously on 12 September 1962. The Council had examined the application of the twin-island Caribbean state, which had become independent from Britain at the end of August that year. Its application was among the first acts of the new government.

The resolution simply recommends that the General Assembly admit Trinidad and Tobago to membership. The brevity is normal for admission cases, where the real decision happened in consultations before the vote. Still, the text marks a clear milestone: a small oil-producing island nation in the southern Caribbean taking its place in the General Assembly for the first time.

A prosecutor's appointment is extended for a final period on 14 September 2007. Carla Del Ponte's term as Prosecutor of the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal was expiring that day, and the Secretary-General had asked for the extension to ensure a smooth handover to her successor. The Council set aside the usual term rule in the tribunal's Statute and extended her appointment from 15 September to 31 December 2007.

The Golan watch came up for its mid-2009 turn. The chief's report of 8 June found the line calm. UNDOF had held its posts since 1974. Its term was days from its end. Resolution 1875 passed on 23 June 2009.

The force gained six months, to 31 December 2009. The Council called on both sides to act on the 1973 text at once. A full clause goes to staff rules. The force must keep faith with the UN's zero-tolerance line. Troop states must drill, probe, and punish as the code asks. A report on events and on steps toward the old text was due at the close. These late renewals read like twins, yet each kept a real force in place through a tense age.

Guinea's complaint against Portugal sits at the heart of Resolution 275, adopted on 22 December 1969 by nine votes to none with six abstentions. Portuguese forces based in the neighboring territory of Guinea-Bissau had shelled Guinean villages, causing deaths and heavy damage. The Council said attacks of this kind put international peace at risk.

Beyond deploring the shelling, the Council ordered Portugal to stop violating Guinea's sovereignty at once. It also demanded the return of a captured Guinean civilian plane, held since March 1968, and of a seized motor barge named Patrice Lumumba, together with everyone taken aboard both. Portugal was warned that repeat attacks would force the Council to weigh stronger steps.

Papua New Guinea is the subject of Resolution 375. The Council passed it by a full vote on 22 September 1975. The Pacific land had won its freedom from Australia six days before, on 16 September. It joined the north and south halves of one big island under a single state.

The Council asks the General Assembly to admit Papua New Guinea as a member. The Assembly then did so. The short text marks the start of a singular state. Its people speak more tongues than any other land on earth. Building one nation from so many groups was a hard task from day one.

Central America's wars were winding down in 1990. A small UN team, known as ONUCA, watched the peace deals hold. Its task was set by a 1989 text. The Secretary-General sent a fresh report on 26 October 1990. Resolution 675 passed on 5 November 1990.

The members backed the report in full. They stretched the team's mandate by six months, to 7 May 1991. They also sent a note of caution. Peacekeeping costs were rising fast across the world. Spending on this mission had to be watched with care. The Secretary-General owed the Council full news of events. A last report was due before the new term ran out.

A small question of costs for the Council's own fact-finding missions was settled on 27 September 1949. Under a General Assembly decision of 1948, the Council could judge whether a member state's representative on such a commission needed an alternate. If the need existed, the Secretary-General could repay travel and living costs. Resolution 75 applies that rule to two real cases.

The Council noted that on two of its commissions, the representatives had each needed an alternate. One was the Committee of Good Offices, by then renamed the United Nations Commission for Indonesia. The other was the United Nations Commission for India and Pakistan. That finding cleared the way for the costs in both cases to be repaid. The text is a minor piece of early United Nations housekeeping, but it shows how even the new body's fact-finding work depended on small rulings about money and staffing.

Haiti's security passes from a US-led coalition to the United Nations in Resolution 975, adopted on 30 January 1995 by fourteen votes to none with China abstaining. The multinational force sent in during 1994 had restored the elected president and reported that a secure and stable environment now existed. Its commander recommended a smooth handover to the UN mission, UNMIH, which the Council had created on paper in 1993.

The Council set the transfer in motion, deciding that UNMIH would deploy with up to six thousand troops and take over from the coalition by the end of March 1995. Haiti's file, crowded with sanctions and authorizations since 1993, now became a peacekeeping operation.
zola-abbe-mouret-1875:
Vizetelly's opening essay places Abbe Mouret's Transgression with care in the saga. Issued fourth, it stands ninth in Zola's final plan for the set. It grows out of The Conquest of Plassans and its wrecked Mouret home.

Serge Mouret, seen as a child there, now serves as priest of Les Artaud. That near-pagan hamlet sits in bare, burning country in Provence. Illness strands him in the wild walled garden of Le Paradou. There he loves the free Albine, and nature wars with the Church in him. Lush and sad, the tale holds one of the finest love stories in the cycle.
